rag-q1.testing: that you see two pipelines with a versioned contract between them, and can say where quality, latency and cost come from.
rag-q1.spoken:
"I'd describe it as two pipelines, not one, because they have different SLAs, scale differently and fail differently.

The offline, ingestion pipeline turns documents into an index: load from the sources, parse — layout-aware for PDFs, so tables and headings survive — chunk by structure, attach metadata like source, section, dates and access permissions, embed the chunks, and write them to the index along with a keyword index for hybrid search. It runs on document changes, and its SLA is freshness: how long until an edited policy is searchable.

The online, serving pipeline answers a question: rewrite the query if it's conversational, retrieve with the user's permission filter applied inside the search, fuse dense and keyword results, rerank the top fifty down to five or so, assemble the prompt with those chunks and their IDs, generate with instructions to cite and to abstain when evidence is missing, and stream the answer with citations. Its SLA is latency and answer quality.

The seam between them is a versioned contract: embedding model, chunking scheme, index and prompt move together. Change one and you re-evaluate, and often re-index.

Around both: caching — embeddings, retrieval results, and a semantic answer cache where it's safe — plus evaluation on a golden set in CI and per-stage tracing in production, so when an answer is wrong I can tell whether retrieval or generation failed."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
• Corpus: size, formats (PDF, HTML, tables), change rate, permissions.
  • Users: query types (lookup, multi-hop, aggregation), languages, QPS.
  • Right: must answers cite? may the system abstain?

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — sizing a mid-size deployment (illustrative):

200k documents × 10 pages × 3 chunks/page      = 6M chunks
6M × 1,024 dims × 4 B (float32)                ≈ 24.6 GB of raw vectors (+ HNSW graph overhead)
   int8 quantised                              ≈ 6.1 GB
Latency budget p95 (target 3 s to last token, TTFT < 1.2 s):
  rewrite 150 ms · retrieve 60 ms · rerank 150 ms · assemble 10 ms · TTFT ~800 ms · stream

stages.name: Baseline design
Deep-dive
stages.html:
Seam Why it matters
embedding model version vectors from two models are incomparable → full re-index on change
chunk scheme changes what "a chunk" means → re-index + re-eval
prompt version changes faithfulness and citation behaviour → re-eval
caches embedding cache (ingest), retrieval cache, semantic answer cache (careful: key on tenant + version)

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Stage Typical failure Signal
parse tables flattened, headers lost wrong answers on table questions
chunk subject severed good recall on keywords, wrong entity
retrieve recall miss / filter mistake low recall@k on golden set
rerank/assemble right chunk buried or truncated recall fine, context relevance low
generate ignores context, no abstention low groundedness

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html: • Add query routing, contextual chunking, GraphRAG or agentic retrieval only when the eval set shows the failure they fix.

followUps.question: 🧪 You change the chunker from 512-token windows to section-based chunks. What else must change?
followUps.html: A full re-index (new chunks → new vectors), a new eval run on the golden set (recall@k and groundedness), possibly the reranker window and the generation top-k, and a version bump of the contract so queries never mix old and new chunks.

followUps.question: "It's basically: embed, search, stuff into the prompt."
followUps.html: That's the demo. Production adds parsing quality, permissions inside retrieval, hybrid search, reranking, citations and abstention, freshness, evaluation and per-stage tracing — that's where the quality and the incidents live.

followUps.question: Why separate ingestion from serving?
followUps.html: Different load (bursty batch vs steady low-latency), different hardware (GPU embedding vs CPU/RAM search), different failures (a bad parse vs a slow query). Separating them lets each scale and fail independently.

followUps.question: Where does the permission check go?
followUps.html: Inside retrieval, as a filter derived from the authenticated user, evaluated during the ANN search — never as a post-filter and never trusted from the prompt (see Q35).

followUps.question: What would you build first with a small team?
followUps.html: A golden set and the simplest pipeline that passes it: good parsing, structure-aware chunks, hybrid retrieval, a reranker, citations. Then tracing and freshness. Advanced patterns only after the eval set shows the gap.

rag-q2.testing: a decision rule by what you're injecting, plus cost shapes.
rag-q2.trap: "fine-tune to add facts" — it teaches form, not knowledge.
rag-q2.spoken:
"I ask what I'm trying to put into the model.

If it's knowledge — documents, policies, product data — especially if it changes, is large, needs citations, or has per-user permissions, that's RAG. The knowledge stays in an index I can update in minutes, delete from, filter by permission and cite.

If it's behaviour — a format, a tone, a domain's way of writing, a narrow task at volume — that's fine-tuning, usually LoRA, after prompting has hit its limit. Fine-tuning is unreliable for facts: the model learns the style of the documents more than their content, can't cite, and must be retrained whenever the content changes.

If it's one document I already have, like a contract to review end to end, long context is simplest: just put it in the prompt.

The cost shapes differ. RAG costs per query: retrieval plus the tokens of the retrieved chunks. Fine-tuning costs up front and again on every data refresh or base-model upgrade. Long context costs every token on every call, plus latency.

In practice the answer is usually RAG, often with a tuned embedding model or reranker for the domain rather than a tuned LLM, and fine-tuning only for a behaviour that prompting can't fix."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Injecting Tool Update path
changing / large / permissioned knowledge RAG re-index a document
behaviour, format, tone, narrow task fine-tune (LoRA) retrain
one document held now long context none

stages.name: Where RAG wins
stages.html: • Freshness in minutes; deletion for compliance; per-user ACLs; citations for trust.

stages.name: Where fine-tuning wins
stages.html:
• Consistent format and style; domain phrasing; smaller model matching a larger one on a narrow task.
  • Domain-tuned embedding model or reranker is often the highest-value fine-tune in a RAG system.

stages.name: Where long context wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — per-query input tokens (illustrative):

RAG:            5 chunks × 400 tokens + 500 prompt   = 2,500 tokens / query
Long context:   a 300-page manual ≈ 150,000 tokens    = 150,000 tokens / query (60×)
Fine-tune:      500 prompt tokens / query, plus a training run per content refresh

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html: • RAG + hybrid retrieval + reranker; fine-tune embeddings/reranker on domain pairs if recall is the gap; LoRA the generator only for format or tone.

followUps.question: 🧪 A policy changes weekly and answers must cite the clause. Which option fails first, and how?
followUps.html: Fine-tuning: it's stale within a week, needs retraining each time, and can't point to a clause. RAG re-indexes the changed policy and cites the chunk ID.

followUps.question: "Fine-tune on our docs so it knows them."
followUps.html: It learns style and some facts unreliably, with no citations and no deletion. Knowledge belongs in retrieval.

followUps.question: Can you combine them?
followUps.html: Yes: RAG for knowledge, a fine-tuned generator for format and grounded behaviour (cite, abstain), and a fine-tuned embedding model for domain recall.

followUps.question: When would long context replace RAG entirely?
followUps.html: Small, stable corpora that fit comfortably and are queried rarely, or tasks needing a whole-document view. Measure quality, TTFT and cost against RAG before switching.

followUps.question: How do you decide with evidence?
followUps.html: Build the golden set first, then compare prompt-only, RAG and (if relevant) fine-tuning on answer quality, faithfulness, cost per query and p95 latency. The decision is a table, not an opinion.

dontSay: A choice without the cost shape.

rag-q3.testing: conceding the true half, then cost, latency, dilution and corpus scale.
rag-q3.spoken:
"Partly, and I'd concede that first. For one long document — a 200-page contract, a codebase snapshot — putting it all in context is now often the right answer, and simpler than building retrieval.

But three things didn't go away. Cost: every token is billed on every call, so a million-token prompt costs hundreds of times more than a focused one. Latency: prefill grows with the prompt, so time to first token goes from under a second to many seconds or more. And quality: models use long contexts unevenly — the middle gets less attention and irrelevant material distracts — so a well-retrieved short context often beats a stuffed one.

And the corpus-size argument ends the debate for most enterprises: ten million documents don't fit in any window, and permissions mean each user may see a different subset anyway.

So long context moved the threshold for when retrieval is needed; it didn't remove the need. The production pattern is retrieve to select, then use a generous window to reason, with prompt caching for large stable prefixes."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: convenience vs cost, latency and precision
stages.html: "Long context raised the size of problem you can solve without retrieval; retrieval still owns large, changing, permissioned corpora."

stages.name: Where long context wins
stages.html:
• Contract review, full-report summarisation, a single codebase question.
  • Small stable corpora with prompt caching.

stages.name: Where RAG still wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the per-query arithmetic (illustrative):

Focused RAG context:      3,000 tokens
Full 1M-token context:    1,000,000 tokens  → ~333× the input tokens per query
Corpus: 10M documents × ~2,000 tokens = 20B tokens → no window holds it
  • Per-user permissions, deletions and daily updates are index operations, not prompt operations.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: does the corpus fit, stay stable, and need no per-user filtering?
stages.html:
• Yes to all three and queries are few → long context is fine.
  • Otherwise → retrieval, possibly with a generous context window.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: retrieve to select, long context to reason
stages.html: • Retrieve more (say 20–50 chunks) with a bigger window than before, reranked; cache stable prefixes; measure against a full-context baseline on the golden set.

followUps.question: 🧪 A 500-page manual (~250k tokens), 2,000 questions a day. Full context or RAG?
followUps.html: 250k × 2,000 = 500M input tokens a day for full context versus ~6M for RAG at 3k per query. Prompt caching narrows the gap but not the latency or dilution. RAG, unless evaluation shows long context answers much better.

followUps.question: "Models handle a million tokens now, so retrieval is legacy."
followUps.html: Accepting a million tokens isn't using them well, and the cost and latency scale with every call. Retrieval is also how you enforce permissions and freshness.

followUps.question: How do long context and RAG work together?
followUps.html: Retrieval selects the relevant material; a larger window lets you pass more of it (parent sections, neighbouring chunks) so the model has enough context to reason. That combination is common now.

followUps.question: How would you test it?
followUps.html: Same golden questions, three setups: RAG top-5, RAG top-30 with a larger window, full context. Compare faithfulness, answer quality, TTFT and cost per query.

followUps.question: What would change your mind?
followUps.html: Much cheaper long-context inference plus evidence that quality holds at full length on our tasks, for a corpus that's small and permission-free. Then retrieval becomes optional for that use case.

rag-q4.testing: measured judgement about when to add a system, and the consistency cost of a second store.
rag-q4.trap: reaching for a vector DB before measuring.
rag-q4.spoken:
"Nothing is wrong with Postgres at small and medium scale. pgvector gives HNSW and IVF indexes, and the big advantage is that vectors live next to the documents, metadata and permissions in one transactional database: joins, filters and deletes are consistent, backups are one system, and the team already operates it.

You outgrow it on three axes. Index size versus memory: HNSW wants the graph in RAM, and at tens of millions of vectors that's a lot of memory on one primary. Filtered search: combining selective metadata filters with ANN — tenant plus date — is where purpose-built engines have better filtered-traversal support. And operations at scale: sharding, rebuilding indexes without downtime, and high query rates.

A dedicated vector store has a hidden cost: a second consistency boundary. Documents and vectors are now in two places, so deletes and permission changes must propagate reliably, or you serve stale or forbidden content.

And sometimes the answer is neither: for keyword-heavy corpora, BM25 in Postgres or OpenSearch is a real baseline.

So I start with pgvector, measure recall and latency with realistic filters on a copy of production data, and move when one of those three axes actually hurts."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: one consistent system vs a specialised engine
stages.html:
pgvector dedicated vector DB
consistency with docs/ACLs ✅ same transaction second boundary to sync
operations existing team, backups new system to run
scale (vectors, QPS) fine to ~millions built for tens/hundreds of millions
filtered ANN improving (iterative scans in recent versions) usually more mature
hybrid search with FTS / extensions often built in

stages.name: Where pgvector wins
stages.html: • Deletes and permission changes are atomic with the source data; joins for metadata; one backup and HA story.

stages.name: Where a dedicated store wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — memory for the HNSW index (illustrative):

20M chunks × 768 dims × 4 B = 61 GB of vectors
+ HNSW graph (M=16 → ~32 neighbour ids × 4–8 B per node) ≈ +2.5–5 GB
→ one Postgres primary with ~70 GB of hot index; int8 or PQ in a dedicated engine ≈ 15 GB or less

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
• Load a realistic sample, run production-like filtered queries, measure recall@10 and p95.
  • Move only when memory, filtered-query latency or re-index operations fail the target.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: pgvector first, with an exit plan
stages.html: • Keep an abstraction over the retriever; store the embedding version per row; design the sync (outbox or CDC) you'll need if a second store arrives.

followUps.question: 🧪 A user's access to a folder is revoked. With vectors in a separate store, what can go wrong?
followUps.html: If ACLs are copied into the vector store as metadata, a delayed sync means their queries can still retrieve those chunks. Either re-check permissions against the source of truth at retrieval time or define and monitor a maximum staleness window.

followUps.question: "RAG needs a vector database."
followUps.html: It needs retrieval. pgvector, OpenSearch/Elasticsearch with kNN, or even BM25 alone can be right. The store is an operational choice, measured, not a requirement.

followUps.question: How do you keep two stores consistent?
followUps.html: Transactional outbox or change-data-capture from the source database; idempotent upserts keyed by chunk ID and version; tombstones for deletes; reconciliation jobs comparing counts and hashes.

followUps.question: Why is filtered ANN hard?
followUps.html: Graph search assumes you can walk to neighbours; a selective filter removes most of them, so naive post-filtering returns too few results and pre-filtering breaks the graph's navigability (see Q28).

followUps.question: When would you choose a managed vector service?
followUps.html: When scale or filtered-search needs exceed Postgres and the team doesn't want to run a new cluster, with data-residency and cost checked. Keep the retrieval interface abstract so the store can change.

dontSay: Adding a vector DB with no sync plan.

rag-q5.testing: short query vs long passage, and that the embedding model must be trained (and prompted) for it.
rag-q5.trap: using a similarity model for search and blaming the chunking.
rag-q5.spoken:
"Symmetric retrieval compares things of the same kind: sentence to sentence, product to product, for deduplication or 'more like this'. Asymmetric retrieval compares a short query — 'refund window for damaged goods' — with a long passage that answers it. That's the normal RAG case.

It matters because the two texts look different: a question is short and phrased as a need; the passage is long and phrased as a statement. A model trained only on symmetric pairs, like paraphrases, puts questions near other questions, not near their answers, so recall drops silently.

Modern embedding models are trained on query–passage pairs and many expect instruction prefixes: for example 'query: ' versus 'passage: ' for E5-style models, or a task instruction on the query side. Forgetting the prefix, or using the wrong one, costs recall without any error message.

So when I pick an embedding model, I check that it's trained for asymmetric retrieval, I apply its prefixes exactly as documented, and I measure recall@k on real questions from our users against our chunks — not on sentence-similarity benchmarks."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Asymmetric retrieval matches a short query to a longer passage that answers it; symmetric matches like with like."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.claim: trained on query–passage pairs, told which side is which
stages.html:
Model family Convention
E5 query: … / passage: … prefixes
BGE (v1.5) instruction prefix on the query for retrieval
instruction-tuned embedders task instruction on the query side
API models often separate input_type / task parameters
  • Contrastive training with in-batch negatives pulls a question toward its answer passage, not toward similar questions.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the eval that catches it (cells to measure):

Setup recall@10 on real queries
symmetric sentence-similarity model measure
retrieval model, no prefixes measure
retrieval model, documented prefixes measure
+ HyDE (hypothetical answer as query) measure
  • Other breakers: queries much shorter than training queries; long chunks beyond the model's trained length.

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.claim: prefixes wrapped in the client, never forgotten
stages.html:
• Always read the model card for prefixes; wrap them in the embedding client so nobody forgets.
  • Keep query and document embedding code paths separate in the codebase.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • HyDE turns the query into an answer-shaped text to close the gap from the query side (Q12).

followUps.question: 🧪 Your team embeds both queries and passages with "passage: " because "it's all text". Effect?
followUps.html: Queries are embedded as if they were passages, so they sit in the passage region shaped by their surface wording rather than the query region the model learned to map to answers; recall usually drops. Fix the prefixes and re-measure recall@k.

followUps.question: "Our chunking is wrong because recall is low."
followUps.html: Check the embedding model and prefixes first: a symmetric model or missing prefixes causes the same symptom and is much cheaper to fix than re-chunking.

followUps.question: Where is symmetric retrieval the right choice?
followUps.html: Duplicate detection, clustering similar tickets, "related articles", finding similar past questions (FAQ matching) — both sides have the same form.

followUps.question: Does a cross-encoder reranker care?
followUps.html: It reads query and passage together, so asymmetry is handled inside the model, but it only reorders what retrieval found. It can't recover passages the bi-encoder missed.

followUps.question: How would you choose between two embedding models?
followUps.html: On a golden set of real user queries and their answering chunks, each model with its documented prefixes: recall@10 and MRR, plus dimension, cost, latency and hosting constraints (see Q22).

dontSay: Picking a model from sentence-similarity benchmarks for search.

rag-q6.testing: a stage-by-stage failure taxonomy with a way to tell them apart.
rag-q6.spoken:
"I name them by pipeline stage, because each has a different fix.

Ingestion: documents missing from the index, bad parsing — tables flattened, headers and footers mixed into text, scanned pages with no OCR. Chunking: the subject severed from its content, so a chunk says 'the limit is 30 days' without saying which product. Retrieval: a recall failure — the right chunk isn't in the top-k, because of vocabulary mismatch, a wrong filter or the wrong embedding model — or a precision failure, where it's there but ranked 40th. Assembly: truncation to fit the budget, the key chunk lost in the middle of a long context, or contradictory versions of the same document. Generation: the model ignores the context and answers from memory, embellishes beyond it, fails to abstain when evidence is missing, or cites the wrong chunk.

Calling all of that hallucination hides the stage. So I diagnose with evidence: recall@k on a golden set separates retrieval from the rest; the RAG triad — context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance — separates ranking and assembly from generation; and per-query traces show which chunks were retrieved and sent.

Then the fix is stage-specific: a better parser, structure-aware chunks, hybrid search, reranking, reordering, or prompt and model changes for grounding."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a failure at a specific stage
stages.html:
Stage Failure Looks like
ingest missing doc, bad parse, no OCR "it doesn't know X"
chunk subject severed, table split wrong entity, wrong number
retrieve recall miss; precision miss irrelevant or incomplete answer
assemble truncated, lost in middle, conflicting versions inconsistent answers
generate ignores context, embellishes, no abstention, bad citation "hallucination"

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: the question and the ground truth
stages.html:
• Was the answer actually in the corpus? (If not: coverage gap, not a model failure.)
  • Is the golden answer current? (Stale ground truth looks like a wrong answer.)
  • Was the question ambiguous? (Answer relevance, not retrieval.)

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the interpretation table:

Evidence Stage First fix
gold chunk not in top-50 retrieval recall hybrid, embedding model, filter check, re-chunk
gold chunk in top-50, not top-5 ranking reranker
gold chunk sent, groundedness low generation grounding prompt, abstention, model
context relevance low, recall fine assembly/ranking rerank, compress, reorder
answers fine, users unhappy answer relevance query rewriting, UX
table questions wrong, prose fine parsing layout-aware extraction

stages.name: Fix by stage
stages.claim: one stage at a time, measured
stages.html: • One stage at a time, measured on the golden set; don't change chunker, model and prompt together.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html: • Recall@k, context relevance, groundedness and answer relevance tracked per release, sliced by query type.

followUps.question: 🧪 Recall@10 is 0.95, groundedness is 0.6. Which stage?
followUps.html: Generation (or assembly): the evidence is retrieved but the answers aren't supported by it. Check whether the chunk reached the prompt (truncation) and then the grounding prompt, abstention rules and model.

followUps.question: "The model hallucinated."
followUps.html: Maybe, but first check whether the right chunk was retrieved and sent. Most "hallucinations" in RAG trace back to parsing, chunking or retrieval.

followUps.question: What's the most common failure you've seen?
followUps.html: Parsing and chunking: tables and headings lost, chunks without their subject. They're invisible in demos with clean text and dominate real corpora.

followUps.question: How do traces help?
followUps.html: A trace per query with the rewritten query, retrieved IDs and scores, reranked order, the final prompt and the answer lets you replay and assign the failure to a stage in minutes.

followUps.question: How do you prioritise fixes across stages?
followUps.html: Classify a sample of failing queries by stage, count them, and fix the biggest bucket first. Re-classify after each change; the distribution shifts.

rag-q7.testing: the layered graph, greedy search, and efSearch as the production recall–latency knob.
rag-q7.spoken:
"HNSW — hierarchical navigable small world — is a graph index. Every vector is a node connected to some of its nearest neighbours. The hierarchy works like a skip list: the top layers contain few nodes with long-range links, and each lower layer contains more nodes, down to the bottom layer, which has all of them.

A search starts at an entry point in the top layer and greedily moves to whichever neighbour is closer to the query, until no neighbour is closer. Then it drops a layer and repeats with finer links, until the bottom layer, where it keeps a candidate list of size efSearch and returns the best k.

It's approximate because greedy search can stop at a local optimum: the true nearest neighbour might be reachable only through a node that looked worse at some step. A bigger candidate list explores more and finds it more often.

That gives the three dials. M, the number of links per node, sets memory and graph quality. efConstruction sets how carefully the graph is built. efSearch is the runtime knob: raise it for recall, lower it for latency, and it can be changed per query without rebuilding.

The weak spots are memory — the vectors and the graph live in RAM — and deletes, which are usually soft: marked nodes stay in the graph until a rebuild or compaction."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: greedy search on a layered neighbour graph
stages.html: "HNSW finds neighbours by greedy descent through a skip-list-like hierarchy of proximity graphs; efSearch trades latency for recall." (Malkov & Yashunin, 2016/2018)

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: layers, greedy descent, a candidate list
stages.html:
Dial Effect
M links per node: memory ↑, recall ↑
efConstruction build effort: build time ↑, graph quality ↑
efSearch query effort: latency ↑, recall ↑ (runtime, per query)

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import numpy as np, faiss
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); d, n, nq = 64, 100_000, 500
xb = rng.normal(size=(n, d)).astype("float32"); xq = rng.normal(size=(nq, d)).astype("float32")
gt = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d); gt.add(xb); _, truth = gt.search(xq, 10)
hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32); hnsw.add(xb)
for ef in (16, 64, 256):
    hnsw.hnsw.efSearch = ef; _, got = hnsw.search(xq, 10)
    print(ef, round(np.mean([len(set(a) & set(b)) / 10 for a, b in zip(got, truth)]), 2))
# → 16 0.39
# → 64 0.71
# → 256 0.93        (faiss-cpu, M-series Mac; query time grew ~12× from 16 to 256)

Random Gaussian vectors are a hard case with no cluster structure; real embeddings reach high recall at lower efSearch. The shape — recall climbing with efSearch at a latency cost — is the point.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: RAM for vectors and graph, and soft deletes
stages.html:
• Memory: vectors + ~M×2 neighbour IDs per node at layer 0, all in RAM.
  • Deletes: soft deletes degrade search and waste memory until rebuild/compaction.
  • Build time: high efConstruction on tens of millions of vectors takes hours.
  • Filters: selective metadata filters break naive graph search (Q28).

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: tune efSearch to a recall target
stages.html:
• Tune efSearch on your data against a recall target (e.g. recall@10 ≥ 0.95 vs exact search) and your latency budget; expose it as config.
  • Monitor recall with periodic exact-search samples; plan compaction if the corpus churns.

followUps.question: 🧪 You raise efSearch from 64 to 256. What happens to recall, latency and memory?
followUps.html: Recall rises, latency rises (roughly with the candidates explored — ~4× more here), and memory doesn't change: efSearch is a search-time parameter, not part of the index.

followUps.question: "HNSW returns the exact nearest neighbours."
followUps.html: It returns approximate ones; greedy search can miss the true nearest. You measure recall against exact search and tune efSearch to the level you need.

followUps.question: Why the hierarchy?
followUps.html: Long-range links in upper layers get the search close to the target in a few hops; lower layers refine. Without them, greedy search on one dense graph takes many more steps.

followUps.question: How do deletes work?
followUps.html: Usually marked deleted and skipped in results but still used for navigation; heavy churn accumulates dead nodes and hurts recall and memory, so indexes are periodically rebuilt or compacted.

followUps.question: When would you not use HNSW?
followUps.html: When the index can't fit in RAM (DiskANN/IVF-PQ), under very high churn (IVF rebuilds more easily), or at small scale where exact search is fast enough and simpler.

spine: Where IVF-PQ and disk indexes win
rag-q8.testing: RAM, recall, churn and build cost as the deciding axes.
rag-q8.trap: treating HNSW as the only index.
rag-q8.spoken:
"They trade recall, memory, build time and how well they handle change.

HNSW is a graph index: best recall-per-latency in memory, but it keeps full vectors plus a graph in RAM, builds slowly, and deletes are soft.

IVF, inverted file, clusters the vectors into cells with k-means, then at query time searches only the nprobe nearest cells. It builds quickly, rebuilds easily, and is simpler under churn, but at the same latency its recall is usually below HNSW, and it needs training on representative data.

IVF-PQ adds product quantisation: each vector is split into sub-vectors and each is replaced by a one-byte code, so a 64-dimension float vector of 256 bytes becomes 16 bytes. That's a huge memory saving, which is what makes billions of vectors affordable, at a recall cost you usually recover by re-scoring the shortlist with full vectors.

When the index can't fit in RAM at all, disk-based indexes like DiskANN keep a compressed copy in memory and full vectors on SSD.

So: HNSW when it fits in memory and quality matters; IVF when churn or rebuild time dominates; IVF-PQ or DiskANN when scale makes memory the constraint. Measure recall against exact search on your data for each."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Index Memory Recall at a given latency Build / rebuild Churn
HNSW highest (vectors + graph) best slow soft deletes accumulate
IVF-Flat vectors + centroids good with enough nprobe fast, needs k-means training easy rebuilds
IVF-PQ ~10–30× smaller lower; recover with rescoring fast easy rebuilds
DiskANN small RAM + SSD high slow improving

stages.name: Where HNSW wins
stages.html: • Up to tens of millions of vectors in RAM; latency-critical; moderate churn.

stages.name: Where IVF wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — IVF vs IVF-PQ recall and bytes (FAISS, measured):

import numpy as np, faiss
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); d, n, nq = 64, 100_000, 500
xb = rng.normal(size=(n, d)).astype("float32"); xq = rng.normal(size=(nq, d)).astype("float32")
gt = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d); gt.add(xb); _, truth = gt.search(xq, 10)
rec = lambda idx: np.mean([len(set(a) & set(b)) / 10 for a, b in zip(idx.search(xq, 10)[1], truth)])
ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(faiss.IndexFlatL2(d), d, 256); ivf.train(xb); ivf.add(xb)
pq = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(faiss.IndexFlatL2(d), d, 256, 16, 8); pq.train(xb); pq.add(xb)
for nprobe in (8, 32):
    ivf.nprobe = pq.nprobe = nprobe; print(nprobe, round(rec(ivf), 2), round(rec(pq), 2))
# → 8 0.24 0.21
# → 32 0.54 0.37            (bytes per vector: 256 flat → 16 with PQ)

On structure-free random data recall is low for both; the trend is what matters: more nprobe buys recall, PQ costs recall and saves 16× memory.

stages.name: Where IVF-PQ and disk indexes win
stages.html:
1B vectors × 768 dims × 4 B = 3 TB raw  → impossible in RAM
PQ at 64 bytes/vector        = 64 GB    → one large machine
  • Rescore the top ~100 PQ candidates with full-precision vectors stored on disk or in a separate store.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html: • < RAM budget, quality first → HNSW. Heavy churn or frequent rebuilds → IVF. Hundreds of millions+ → IVF-PQ/DiskANN with rescoring. Always verify recall@10 vs exact search.

followUps.question: 🧪 768-dim float32 vectors, PQ with 96 sub-quantisers at 8 bits. Compression ratio?
followUps.html: 768 × 4 = 3,072 bytes → 96 bytes: 32× smaller (plus a small codebook shared by all vectors).

followUps.question: "HNSW is always the best index."
followUps.html: Best in memory at moderate scale. At large scale memory cost dominates, and under heavy churn rebuild friendliness matters; IVF-PQ or DiskANN win there.

followUps.question: What does nprobe do?
followUps.html: The number of IVF cells searched. More cells → higher recall, higher latency. It's IVF's equivalent of efSearch.

followUps.question: Why does IVF need training?
followUps.html: The cell centroids come from k-means on a sample of vectors. If the data distribution shifts (new domain, new embedding model), cells become unbalanced and recall drops, so retrain periodically.

followUps.question: How would you choose for 300M chunks on a budget?
followUps.html: IVF-PQ or DiskANN with float rescoring of a shortlist, possibly Matryoshka-truncated or int8 vectors; shard by tenant or time; benchmark recall@10 and p95 on a production-like sample before committing.

dontSay: Quoting recall without comparing to exact search.

rag-q9.testing: why cross-encoders can't scale (no precompute) and the retrieve-many-rerank-few pattern.
rag-q9.trap: not explaining why the cross-encoder can't search the whole corpus.
rag-q9.spoken:
"A bi-encoder encodes the query and each document separately into vectors, and relevance is their dot product. Because documents are encoded independently, all their vectors can be computed once, offline, and searched with an ANN index in milliseconds over millions of chunks. The limit is accuracy: the query and document never see each other, so subtle relevance — negation, which entity, which date — is compressed away.

A cross-encoder reads the query and document together in one transformer pass, with full attention between them, and outputs a relevance score. That's much more accurate, but nothing can be precomputed: every query–document pair needs a fresh forward pass. Scoring a million chunks per query is impossible; scoring fifty is fine.

So you run both: the bi-encoder, often with BM25, retrieves the top fifty to a hundred for recall, and the cross-encoder reranks them and keeps the top five or so for precision. Because the reranked top five is much more relevant, you can send fewer chunks to the LLM, which often pays back the rerank latency.

ColBERT-style late interaction sits between: per-token vectors precomputed, scored with token-level matching, better than a bi-encoder, at a large storage cost."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Bi-encoder Cross-encoder
input query and doc separately query + doc together
precompute docs ✅ offline vectors ❌ nothing reusable
cost per query 1 query encoding + ANN 1 forward pass per candidate
accuracy good recall, coarse ranking high precision
role retrieval reranking

stages.name: Where the bi-encoder wins
stages.html: • Millions of chunks searched in milliseconds; embeddings cached; index-friendly.

stages.name: Where the cross-encoder wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — compute per query (illustrative):

Corpus 5M chunks
Bi-encoder:     1 query encode + ANN over precomputed vectors      ≈ tens of ms
Cross-encoder over the whole corpus: 5,000,000 forward passes     → impossible online
Cross-encoder over top-50:            50 forward passes, batched  ≈ 50–200 ms on a GPU

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: is the right chunk retrieved but ranked low?
stages.html:
• recall@50 high, precision@5 low → add a reranker.
  • recall@50 low → the reranker can't help; fix retrieval (Q44).

stages.name: What I'd pick

followUps.question: 🧪 Reranking 100 candidates takes 300 ms. What's your first latency lever?
followUps.html: Rerank fewer candidates (e.g. 100 → 30) if recall@30 is still near recall@100 on the golden set; then a smaller or distilled reranker, batching, and GPU placement.

followUps.question: "Just use the cross-encoder for retrieval, it's more accurate."
followUps.html: It needs a forward pass per document per query and can't use an index, so it can't search a corpus. It only works on a shortlist.

followUps.question: Can an LLM be the reranker?
followUps.html: Yes, listwise or pointwise LLM reranking works well, but it's slower and costlier than a dedicated cross-encoder. Use it where quality justifies it or for low QPS.

followUps.question: Why does reranking often reduce total latency?
followUps.html: Better precision lets you send 5 chunks instead of 15 to the LLM, cutting prefill time and tokens, which can outweigh the rerank cost.

followUps.question: Would you fine-tune the reranker?
followUps.html: If domain relevance differs from general web relevance (legal, medical, internal jargon) and you have labelled or mined query–chunk pairs. A tuned reranker is often a bigger win than a tuned LLM.

dontSay: "Cross-encoders are better, so use them for retrieval."
Adding a reranker when recall is the problem.

rag-q10.testing: that score scales are incomparable and drift, and that rank fusion avoids calibration.
rag-q10.trap: proposing weighted fusion without mentioning calibration drift.
rag-q10.spoken:
"Hybrid search runs dense retrieval, which is good at meaning and paraphrase, and sparse keyword retrieval like BM25, which is good at exact tokens: product codes, error strings, names, rare jargon. Then you have to merge two ranked lists.

A weighted blend of scores — say 0.7 times cosine plus 0.3 times BM25 — assumes the two scores are on comparable scales. They aren't: cosine lives in a narrow band that depends on the embedding model, and BM25 is unbounded and depends on query length and corpus statistics. The right weights change per query, per corpus and whenever you swap a model, so you're maintaining a calibration forever.

Reciprocal rank fusion ignores the scores and uses only the ranks: each document gets one over k plus its rank from each list, summed, with k usually 60. A document ranked highly by both wins; a document found by only one still gets in. There's nothing to calibrate, and it's robust when you change a retriever.

A tuned weighted blend can beat RRF if you normalise scores and learn the weights on a labelled set, and you keep re-tuning. Most teams don't, so RRF is my default, and I measure whether hybrid helps at all: it matters most on identifier-heavy corpora."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Score fusion needs calibrated, comparable scores; rank fusion needs only the order each retriever produced."

RRF(d) = Σ_r 1 / (k + rank_r(d)), k ≈ 60 (Cormack et al., 2009)

stages.name: Where RRF wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — fusing two lists:

dense = ["d7", "d2", "d9", "d4", "d1"]           # ranked by cosine
bm25  = ["d4", "d8", "d7", "d3", "d2"]           # ranked by BM25
def rrf(*lists, k=60):
    s = {}
    for L in lists:
        for r, doc in enumerate(L, 1): s[doc] = s.get(doc, 0) + 1 / (k + r)
    return sorted(s, key=s.get, reverse=True)
print(rrf(dense, bm25)[:5])
# → ['d7', 'd4', 'd2', 'd8', 'd9']

d7 and d4 appear high in both lists and rise to the top; d8, found only by BM25 (an exact-token hit), still makes the shortlist.

stages.name: Where a weighted blend wins
stages.html: • Normalised scores (min-max or z-score per query) plus weights learned on a labelled set can outperform RRF — until a model or corpus change shifts the distributions.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: can you afford to keep a calibration current?
stages.html: • No → RRF. Yes, with labels and CI evals → tuned blend or a learned fusion/reranker.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html: • RRF to merge, cross-encoder to order the fused top-50; measure dense-only vs hybrid recall@k first (Q23).

followUps.question: 🧪 With k = 60, a doc ranked 1st by dense only vs a doc ranked 3rd by both. Which wins?
followUps.html: 1/61 ≈ 0.0164 vs 2/63 ≈ 0.0317: the doc found by both wins. RRF rewards agreement between retrievers.

followUps.question: "Just add the scores."
followUps.html: Cosine and BM25 scales differ and shift per query and per model; raw sums let one retriever dominate unpredictably. Normalise and tune, or fuse ranks.

followUps.question: What does k control?
followUps.html: How much top ranks dominate. Small k makes the first positions count much more; large k flattens the differences. 60 is a robust default from the original paper.

followUps.question: Where does sparse retrieval beat dense?
followUps.html: Exact identifiers (SKUs, error codes, ticket IDs), rare names and new jargon the embedding model never saw (see Q55).

followUps.question: How would you roll out hybrid search?
followUps.html: Measure recall@k and answer quality on the golden set, sliced by query type (ID-heavy vs natural language), dense-only vs hybrid; ship if the gain is real on important slices; watch p95 because two retrievers run per query.

dontSay: Fusing without a reranker or an eval.

rag-q11.testing: the lost-subject problem, and the difference between prepending text and pooling embeddings.
rag-q11.spoken:
"Both fix the same problem: a chunk loses the context that makes it findable. A chunk that says 'revenue grew 3 percent over the previous quarter' doesn't say which company or which quarter, so a query about 'Acme's Q2 revenue' can't match it, and BM25 can't either.

Contextual chunking, popularised by Anthropic in 2024, uses an LLM at ingestion: for each chunk, give it the whole document and ask for a short blurb that situates the chunk — 'This is from Acme's Q2 2024 report, discussing revenue.' Prepend that to the chunk before embedding it and before indexing it for BM25. Anthropic reported that retrieval failures dropped substantially, and more when combined with BM25 and reranking.

Late chunking, from Jina in 2024, works in embedding space instead: run a long-context embedding model over the whole document first, so every token's representation has seen the full document, then pool the token vectors per chunk. Each chunk's vector carries document context without any added text.

Costs differ: contextual chunking is one LLM call per chunk at ingest — prompt caching of the document makes that much cheaper; late chunking needs a long-context embedding model and doesn't help BM25.

I'd try the cheap fix first — prepend the document title and section path as metadata — measure recall, then add contextual chunking if the eval shows lost-subject failures."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: restore the chunk's missing context before indexing
stages.html: "Contextual chunking prepends LLM-written context text; late chunking embeds the whole document first and pools per chunk."

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: one adds text, the other pools embeddings
stages.html:
Contextual chunking Late chunking
where context is added text prepended to the chunk token embeddings computed with full-document attention
helps BM25 ✅ (the blurb has the keywords) ❌
ingest cost 1 LLM call per chunk (cacheable doc prefix) 1 long-context embedding pass per document
model requirement any LLM + any embedder long-context embedding model

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Chunk (as split):
  "Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter, driven by services."
Contextualised chunk (embedded and BM25-indexed):
  "From Acme Corp's Q2 2024 quarterly report, section Financial Results.
   Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter, driven by services."
Query: "How did Acme's revenue change in Q2 2024?"
  → the first version shares almost no identifying terms with the query; the second does.

Eval to run (cells to measure):

Variant recall@20 answer faithfulness
plain chunks measure measure
+ title/section metadata prefix measure measure
+ contextual chunking measure measure
+ contextual + BM25 + rerank measure measure

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: ingest LLM calls or a long-context embedder
stages.html:
• Contextual: LLM tokens ≈ (document tokens + chunk tokens) per chunk; with prompt caching the document part is billed at a cached rate. Re-run when documents change.
  • Late: long-context embedding model limits (e.g. 8k tokens); longer documents need splitting anyway.
  • Both: a re-index, and a version bump of the chunking contract.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: free metadata first, contextual chunks where evals show lost subjects
stages.html:
• Start with free context: title, section path, dates as prefix and metadata.
  • Add contextual chunking where the golden set shows chunks losing their subject (reports, contracts, long manuals).

followUps.question: 🧪 A 50-page document split into 200 chunks. Contextual chunking without prompt caching — rough LLM input tokens?
followUps.html: About 200 × (25,000 document tokens + chunk) ≈ 5M input tokens for one document. With prompt caching, the 25k-token document prefix is cached after the first call, so most of those tokens are billed at the cached rate.

followUps.question: "Contextual and late chunking are the same thing."
followUps.html: Contextual adds text written by an LLM; late chunking changes how embeddings are computed. Only contextual helps keyword search.

followUps.question: Why not just use bigger chunks?
followUps.html: Bigger chunks average several topics into one vector and dilute the match, and they cost more context at generation. Adding context text keeps chunks small and specific (Q16).

followUps.question: Does the blurb go into the prompt too?
followUps.html: Optional. It helps retrieval; in the prompt, the section path is useful, but the generated blurb can be dropped to save tokens.

followUps.question: Would you apply it to the whole corpus?
followUps.html: To the document types where the eval shows lost-subject failures; skip self-contained content like FAQs. Budget the ingest cost and re-run cost for frequently changing documents.

rag-q12.testing: the query–document shape gap, and when an extra LLM call is worth it.
rag-q12.trap: using HyDE where a cheap query rewrite would do.
rag-q12.spoken:
"HyDE — hypothetical document embeddings, from Gao and colleagues in 2022 — attacks the gap between what a query looks like and what an answer looks like. A query is short and phrased as a question; the passages in the index are longer, declarative and full of domain vocabulary. Their embeddings can land in different regions, especially with weaker or symmetric embedding models or jargon-heavy corpora.

So instead of embedding the query, you ask an LLM to write a hypothetical answer — a plausible paragraph, which may be factually wrong — and embed that. The fake answer has the shape and vocabulary of real answers, so it lands near them, and you retrieve real passages with it. The LLM's facts don't matter; only its phrasing does.

It helps most on short or vague queries, zero-shot domains with no fine-tuned embedder, and specialist vocabulary.

The costs: an extra LLM call before retrieval — hundreds of milliseconds — and a risk: if the question has a false premise or the LLM guesses the wrong topic, the fake answer drags retrieval toward the wrong area. Modern asymmetric embedding models close much of the gap already.

So I test it against cheaper options — the model's query prefix, a simple rewrite, multi-query — on the golden set, and use it only on query types where it measurably helps."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: search with a fake answer, not the question
stages.html: "HyDE embeds an LLM-written hypothetical answer so the query vector lands among real answers."

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: embed a fake answer, retrieve real passages
stages.html: • Variants: several hypothetical answers averaged; combine with the original query embedding.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Query:         "why does my pod keep restarting?"
HyDE text:     "A pod restarts repeatedly when its container exits or fails liveness probes.
                Common causes are OOMKilled (exit code 137), a crashing entrypoint, or a
                misconfigured probe. Check `kubectl describe pod` for Last State and events."
→ the second text shares the vocabulary of runbook passages (OOMKilled, liveness probe, exit code 137);
  the query shares almost none of it.
Setup recall@10 (golden set) p95 added
query + model prefix measure 0
rewrite measure measure
HyDE measure measure

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: an extra LLM call and wrong-premise drift
stages.html:
• One LLM call per query (latency and tokens).
  • Wrong-premise amplification: the fake answer can steer retrieval toward the wrong topic.
  • Less benefit with strong asymmetric embedding models.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: route it to the query types it helps
stages.html: • Route: use HyDE only for query classes that benefit (short, jargon, zero-shot domain); skip for ID lookups and well-formed questions.

followUps.question: 🧪 The hypothetical answer contains a wrong fact. Does that break HyDE?
followUps.html: Usually not: retrieval only needs the right vocabulary and topic, and generation uses the real passages. It breaks when the fake answer is on the wrong topic entirely, e.g. a false-premise question.

followUps.question: "HyDE always improves retrieval."
followUps.html: It helps specific query types and adds latency; with good asymmetric embedders the gain can vanish. Measure per query class.

followUps.question: HyDE vs query rewriting?
followUps.html: Rewriting produces a better query; HyDE produces an answer-shaped text. Rewriting is cheaper and safer for vague or conversational queries; HyDE targets the vocabulary gap.

followUps.question: Does HyDE help BM25?
followUps.html: It can: the hypothetical answer adds domain terms, acting like query expansion. It also adds noise terms, so fuse with the original query results.

followUps.question: How would you ship it safely?
followUps.html: Behind a router, for the query classes the eval supports, with a timeout that falls back to the plain query, and metrics on the latency added and recall gained.

dontSay: "HyDE generates the answer we show the user."

rag-q13.testing: that MMR buys coverage by penalising redundancy, and that it's not a reranker.
rag-q13.spoken:
"Pure top-k by similarity often returns near-duplicates: the same paragraph from three versions of a document, or five chunks that all say the same thing. You spend five context slots and get one fact.

Maximal marginal relevance, from Carbonell and Goldstein in 1998, selects chunks one at a time. At each step it picks the candidate that maximises lambda times its relevance to the query minus one minus lambda times its highest similarity to anything already selected. So a chunk that's relevant but repeats what you already have gets penalised, and a relevant chunk covering a different aspect gets in.

Lambda sets the balance: one is pure relevance; lower values push diversity. Too low and you pull in off-topic chunks just because they're different.

It's useful for multi-aspect questions — 'compare the plans' — summarisation over many sources, and corpora full of duplicates. It isn't a precision tool: it doesn't judge relevance better, it just avoids redundancy. That's the reranker's job. And if duplicates come from the corpus itself, deduplicating at ingestion is the better fix."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "MMR(d) = λ·sim(d, q) − (1 − λ)·max sim(d, selected); pick greedily to cover more with the same k."

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: greedy selection over a candidate pool
stages.html:
• Retrieve a larger pool (e.g. 30), then greedily pick k with the MMR score.
  • λ ≈ 0.5–0.7 is a typical starting range; tune on multi-aspect questions.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: top-k picks a duplicate, MMR doesn't
stages.html:
import numpy as np
q = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
docs = {"A": [0.95, 0.31], "A'": [0.94, 0.34], "B": [0.80, -0.60], "C": [0.30, 0.95]}
V = {k: np.array(v) / np.linalg.norm(v) for k, v in docs.items()}
def mmr(k=2, lam=0.5):
    picked = []
    while len(picked) < k:
        best = max((d for d in V if d not in picked), key=lambda d: lam * V[d] @ q - (1 - lam) * max([V[d] @ V[p] for p in picked], default=0))
        picked.append(best)
    return picked
print("top-k:", sorted(V, key=lambda d: -(V[d] @ q))[:2], " MMR:", mmr())
# → top-k: ['A', "A'"]  MMR: ['A', 'B']

A' is almost identical to A; MMR swaps it for B, which is still relevant but covers something different.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: a λ to tune; no relevance gain
stages.html:
• Pairwise similarities over the pool (cheap for tens of candidates).
  • A tuning knob (λ) that can drift off-topic.
  • Doesn't fix bad relevance ordering.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: dedupe first, rerank for precision, MMR for coverage
stages.html: • Dedupe at ingestion first; use MMR for multi-aspect and summary queries; rerank for precision. Order: retrieve → rerank → (optionally) MMR on the reranked pool.

followUps.question: 🧪 With λ = 1, what does MMR return?
followUps.html: Exactly the top-k by relevance: the redundancy term has zero weight. With λ = 0 it ignores relevance and picks maximally different chunks, which is useless.

followUps.question: "MMR is a reranker."
followUps.html: It reorders for diversity using the same similarity scores; it doesn't judge relevance better. A cross-encoder reranker improves relevance.

followUps.question: When does MMR hurt?
followUps.html: Single-fact lookups: the best answer might appear in several near-identical chunks and MMR pushes in less relevant ones. Use it by query type.

followUps.question: Why not just deduplicate?
followUps.html: Exact and near-duplicate removal at ingestion should come first. MMR also handles chunks that are different text but say the same thing for this query.

followUps.question: How would you evaluate adding MMR?
followUps.html: On multi-aspect questions in the golden set: coverage of required facts in the retrieved set and answer completeness, compared with plain top-k at the same k, plus a check that single-fact questions don't regress.

dontSay: λ with no mention of tuning.

rag-q14.testing: decoupling the unit you match from the unit you send.
rag-q14.trap: answering "what chunk size?" with a number instead of this.
rag-q14.spoken:
"Chunk size has a built-in conflict. Small chunks match precisely, because each vector means one thing, but a small chunk often lacks enough context to answer. Large chunks have the context but embed poorly, because the vector averages several topics.

Small-to-big retrieval stops treating those as one unit. You index small units for matching — sentences, or small child chunks — and each keeps a pointer to a larger parent: the surrounding window, the section, or the whole document. Retrieval matches on the small units, then you send the parents to the LLM.

Variants: sentence-window retrieval returns a few sentences around the hit; child-to-parent returns the section; summary-to-document indexes a summary and returns the full document.

The costs: you store the mapping, several children may point to the same parent so you must deduplicate, and parents can blow the context budget, so you cap how many and how large. It also pairs naturally with a reranker, which should score the parent text that the LLM will actually see."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "Index fine-grained units for precise matching; return their larger parents for enough context to answer."

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Variant Match on Send
sentence window sentence ± N sentences
child → parent 128-token chunk enclosing section
summary → document document summary full document (short docs only)

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Children: 128 tokens · Parents: 1,000-token sections
Top-10 children → 6 unique parents after dedupe → 6,000 tokens of context
Cap at 3 parents after reranking → 3,000 tokens: within budget, full clauses intact

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html:
• Mapping storage and a second lookup; dedupe logic.
  • Context budget pressure from large parents.
  • Parents should respect structure (sections), not arbitrary windows.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html: • Default for structured documents: children for matching, sections as parents, rerank on parents, cap by tokens.

followUps.question: 🧪 Five of the top-10 children belong to the same parent section. What do you send?
followUps.html: That parent once, deduplicated — which frees budget for other parents. The repeated hits are also a relevance signal for that section.

followUps.question: "Just use 512-token chunks with 10% overlap."
followUps.html: That picks one compromise for both matching and context. Small-to-big avoids the compromise; if you must use one size, choose it on the golden set, not by convention.

followUps.question: Which does the reranker score, child or parent?
followUps.html: Preferably the parent text the LLM will see, within the reranker's input limit; otherwise the child plus a short parent context.

followUps.question: How does this relate to contextual chunking?
followUps.html: Both fix missing context: contextual chunking fixes it at match time by adding context to the chunk; small-to-big fixes it at answer time by sending the larger unit. They combine well.

followUps.question: When would you not do this?
followUps.html: Short, self-contained documents like FAQs or product cards, where each chunk already is the whole answer. The extra lookup and mapping add nothing.

dontSay: Sending parents without deduplication or a token cap.
Arbitrary windows as parents in structured docs.

rag-q15.testing: per-token vectors, MaxSim, precomputation, and the storage price.
rag-q15.spoken:
"ColBERT, from Khattab and Zaharia in 2020, sits between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder. Instead of one vector per chunk, it keeps a vector for every token of the chunk, and one per token of the query. The score is MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity with any document token, then sum those maxima.

That gives token-level matching — a query term can find the specific phrase that matches it — which captures much of the cross-encoder's precision. But unlike a cross-encoder, the document side is still computed offline, because query and document are encoded separately; they only interact at the scoring step, which is why it's called late interaction.

The price is storage: a 200-token chunk becomes 200 vectors instead of one. ColBERTv2 and PLAID reduce that with compression and centroid-based candidate generation, but it's still much bigger than a single-vector index.

So it fits either as a first-stage retriever when quality matters and storage is affordable, or as a reranker over a shortlist, where the storage cost is irrelevant. Many teams use a cross-encoder for reranking instead, which is simpler."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: many vectors per chunk, matched late
stages.html: "ColBERT keeps per-token embeddings and scores with Σ over query tokens of the max similarity to any document token."

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Bi-encoder ColBERT Cross-encoder
doc representation 1 vector 1 vector per token none (joint pass)
precompute docs ✅ ✅ ❌
interaction dot product MaxSim per query token full attention
storage small large none
quality good better best

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
5M chunks × 1 vector × 768 dims × 2 B (fp16)       ≈ 7.7 GB   (single-vector)
5M chunks × 200 token vectors × 128 dims × 2 B     ≈ 256 GB  (ColBERT, uncompressed)
ColBERTv2 residual compression (~2 bits/dim)        ≈ tens of GB

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html:
• Storage and memory at corpus scale; more complex serving (PLAID engine or specialised stores).
  • Query-time compute higher than single-vector ANN.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: best as a reranker on a shortlist
stages.html:
• As a reranker on a top-100 shortlist: quality near a cross-encoder with fast scoring.
  • As a retriever: consider when single-vector recall is the bottleneck and storage is affordable.

followUps.question: 🧪 Query has 8 tokens, document 200. How many similarity computations does MaxSim need?
followUps.html: 8 × 200 = 1,600 dot products, then 8 maxima summed. Cheap per document, which is why it can score large candidate sets quickly — unlike a cross-encoder's full transformer pass.

followUps.question: "ColBERT is just a better embedding model."
followUps.html: It's a different representation: many vectors per chunk and a different scoring function. That's where both the quality and the storage cost come from.

followUps.question: Why is it called late interaction?
followUps.html: Query and document are encoded separately (like a bi-encoder); they interact only at scoring time (MaxSim), unlike a cross-encoder where they interact in every layer.

followUps.question: Is there a multimodal use?
followUps.html: Yes: ColPali applies late interaction to page images, matching query tokens against image-patch vectors, useful for visually rich PDFs without OCR.

followUps.question: Cross-encoder or ColBERT as your reranker?
followUps.html: Cross-encoder by default: simpler, widely available, strong. ColBERT when reranking larger candidate sets quickly matters, or when you already run it as a retriever. Decide on the golden set and latency budget.

dontSay: Adopting it without comparing to bi-encoder + reranker.

rag-q16.testing: both failure modes, the coupling to the embedding model, and dodging the trade-off.
rag-q16.trap: quoting "512 tokens, 10% overlap" as if it were a law.
rag-q16.spoken:
"I don't start with a number; I start with the documents and the questions.

Too small, and each chunk retrieves precisely but can't answer: the definition is in one chunk and the exception in the next, so the model fills the gap with a guess. Pronouns and references point to text that isn't there.

Too big, and the embedding averages several topics into one blurry vector, so recall drops for any single topic; the chunk wastes context budget; and long contexts dilute the model's attention.

The size also couples to the embedding model: past its trained length, input is silently truncated, and many models are trained on passages of a few hundred tokens.

So three moves. Split on the document's structure first — headings, sections, clauses, table boundaries — rather than on character counts. Then dodge the trade-off with small-to-big retrieval: match on small units, send their parent sections. And tune what's left on the golden set: try two or three sizes, measure recall@k and answer faithfulness, and pick.

Chunk size is part of a versioned contract with the embedding model and the prompt, so changing it means a re-index and a re-eval."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html: "Small chunks match sharply but lack context; big chunks carry context but match blurrily."

stages.name: What breaks when too small
stages.html: • Severed definitions and exceptions; dangling pronouns; more chunks to rank and more noise.

stages.name: What breaks when too big
stages.html: • Multi-topic averaging lowers recall; silent truncation past the embedder's limit; fewer chunks fit in context.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: what does one answer need, and what does the model accept?
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the tuning run (cells to measure on the golden set):

Chunking recall@10 faithfulness avg context tokens
fixed 256 measure measure measure
fixed 1,024 measure measure measure
structure-aware sections measure measure measure
small-to-big (128 → section) measure measure measure

stages.name: What I'd do
stages.html: • Structure-aware splitting; children ~100–300 tokens for matching; sections as parents; tune on the golden set; version with the embedding model.

followUps.question: 🧪 Your embedding model's max input is 512 tokens and your chunks are 1,000. What happens?
followUps.html: Most libraries truncate silently: only the first 512 tokens are embedded, so anything in the second half is unfindable by dense search. Check the model's limit and chunk below it.

followUps.question: "512 tokens with 10% overlap is best practice."
followUps.html: It's a common default, not a law. The right size depends on the documents, the embedding model and the questions; measure it.

followUps.question: Does overlap help?
followUps.html: It reduces cut-in-the-middle losses for fixed-size splitting at the cost of storage and duplicate hits. Structure-aware splitting and small-to-big make it less necessary.

followUps.question: Tables?
followUps.html: Never split a table across chunks without its header; serialise tables as their own chunks with caption and header row (Q50).

followUps.question: How often would you revisit chunking?
followUps.html: When the embedding model changes, a new document type arrives, or eval failures cluster on lost-context errors. It's a versioned decision with a re-index cost, so change it deliberately.

rag-q17.testing: the recall-healthy/precision-poor signature, and latency trade-offs.
rag-q17.trap: adding a reranker when the real failure is recall.
rag-q17.spoken:
"I add a reranker when the evidence shows a specific signature: recall at 50 is healthy — the right chunk is in the candidate pool — but precision at 5 is poor, because it's ranked 20th or 40th. That's exactly what a cross-encoder fixes, and nothing else fixes it as cheaply.

If recall at 50 is low, a reranker can't help: it only reorders what retrieval found. Then I fix retrieval — hybrid search, the embedding model, filters, chunking.

It isn't worth it when the latency budget can't absorb 50 to 200 milliseconds — voice products, autocomplete — when retrieval is already precise, as with small clean corpora, or when a third-party reranking API is unacceptable for data reasons and self-hosting isn't justified.

Two things soften the cost. The number of candidates is the main latency lever: reranking 30 instead of 100 is often enough if recall at 30 is close to recall at 100. And better precision lets me send fewer chunks to the LLM — five instead of fifteen — which cuts prefill time and token cost, so the net latency can go down."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: precision gain vs latency and dependency
stages.html: "A reranker converts a good candidate pool into a good top-5; it can't create candidates."

stages.name: Where a reranker wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the diagnostic (golden set, cells to measure):

Metric Without reranker With reranker
recall@50 measure (must already be high) same
precision@5 / MRR measure measure
faithfulness measure measure
chunks sent to LLM 15 5
p95 end-to-end measure measure

stages.name: Where it isn't worth it
stages.claim: tight budgets, recall problems, small clean corpora
stages.html: • Voice/real-time; recall failures; already-precise retrieval; data-residency blocks on APIs.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: where is the gold chunk ranked today?
stages.html: • Median rank of the gold chunk on the golden set: within top-50 but beyond top-5 → rerank. Beyond top-50 → retrieval work.

stages.name: What I'd do
stages.claim: rerank a right-sized pool, then shrink generation k
stages.html: • Rerank top-30 to 50 (sized by recall plateau), send 3–5 to the LLM, measure p95 and quality together.

followUps.question: 🧪 Recall@50 = 0.55, precision@5 = 0.3. Add a reranker?
followUps.html: Not first. With recall at 0.55, almost half the time the gold chunk isn't even in the pool, so the reranker's ceiling is 0.55. Fix recall (hybrid, embedder, chunking), then add reranking.

followUps.question: "A reranker always improves quality."
followUps.html: Only when the right chunks are in the candidate pool and ranked badly. Otherwise it adds latency and cost for nothing.

followUps.question: Which reranker?
followUps.html: A cross-encoder (open models like BGE-reranker, or hosted rerank APIs) chosen on the golden set for quality, latency and hosting constraints. LLM reranking for low-QPS, high-value queries.

followUps.question: Can you skip reranking for easy queries?
followUps.html: Yes: route exact lookups (IDs, known-item queries) straight through, and rerank only natural-language questions. Saves latency on a large share of traffic.

followUps.question: How do you keep reranker latency under control at scale?
followUps.html: Batch on GPU, cap candidates, truncate passages to the model's window, cache for repeated queries, and consider a distilled smaller reranker; monitor rerank p95 as its own span.

dontSay: Adding a reranker to fix recall.
Ignoring the chance to send fewer chunks.

rag-q18.testing: that good recall rules out the retriever, and that the RAG triad splits what remains.
rag-q18.spoken:
"Good recall rules out the retriever, so I'd say that first: the evidence is being found. The problem is between the candidate pool and the answer, and there are three suspects.

Ranking: the right chunk is in the top 50 but ranked 30th, so it never reaches the prompt. Assembly: it's selected but truncated to fit the budget, placed in the middle of a long context where it's under-used, or sitting next to a contradicting older version. Generation: it's in the prompt, but the model ignores it, answers from its own memory, embellishes, or answers a slightly different question.

I split them with evidence. First, per-query traces: was the gold chunk in the final prompt? If not, it's ranking or assembly. Then the RAG triad on the golden set: context relevance measures whether what we sent is relevant; groundedness, or faithfulness, measures whether the answer is supported by what we sent; answer relevance measures whether it addresses the question. High context relevance with low groundedness means generation. Low context relevance despite good recall means ranking or assembly. High groundedness with unhappy users means answer relevance — the query needs rewriting or the UX needs work.

Fixes follow: a reranker and smaller generation k for ranking; reordering, dedup and version filtering for assembly; a grounding prompt with citations and abstention, or a stronger model, for generation."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "Recall says the evidence was found; the failure is ranking, assembly or generation."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
• Recall@50 on the golden set, or on a proxy? Is the golden set representative of failing traffic?
  • Is the "right" chunk current, or is a stale version the one retrieved?

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the interpretation table:

Gold chunk in prompt? Context relevance Groundedness Answer relevance Stage
no low — — ranking (buried) or assembly (truncated)
yes high low — generation
yes low high — assembly: noise and conflicts diluting it
yes high high low question understanding → rewrite / UX

stages.name: Fix by stage
stages.claim: each stage has its own fix
stages.html:
Stage Fix
ranking cross-encoder rerank, then send fewer chunks
assembly budget by tokens, reorder best to edges, dedupe, filter superseded versions
generation "answer only from sources, cite chunk IDs, abstain otherwise"; lower temperature; stronger model
answer relevance query rewriting, clarification questions

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: re-run the triad on the failing slice
stages.html: • Re-run the triad and end-to-end correctness on the golden set; confirm on the failing slice, not just the average.

followUps.question: 🧪 Recall@50 = 0.93, context relevance 0.4, groundedness 0.9. Diagnosis?
followUps.html: The model sticks to what it's given (groundedness high), but what it's given is mostly noise (context relevance low) — a ranking/assembly problem. Rerank and send fewer, better chunks.

followUps.question: "Recall is fine, so let's re-chunk."
followUps.html: Re-chunking changes retrieval, which is already working. Look at what happens after retrieval first.

followUps.question: How is groundedness measured?
followUps.html: Split the answer into claims; for each, a judge model (or NLI model) checks whether the provided context supports it; score = supported claims / total (Q59). Calibrate the judge on human labels.

followUps.question: Why would a model ignore good context?
followUps.html: Its parametric knowledge conflicts with the context, the context is long and the fact is mid-window, or instructions don't make grounding the priority. Explicit citation requirements and shorter, reordered context help.

followUps.question: How do you prevent this regression coming back?
followUps.html: Component metrics in CI (recall@k, context relevance, groundedness) plus traces in production with the gold-in-prompt check on sampled failures; alerts on groundedness drops by prompt/model version.

dontSay: Fixing generation before checking the chunk reached the prompt.

rag-q19.testing: multi-hop as the real trigger, the costs of a loop, and adaptive routing as the middle ground.
rag-q19.spoken:
"In a fixed pipeline, retrieval happens once, in a set order: rewrite, retrieve, rerank, generate. In agentic RAG, retrieval becomes a tool the model calls in a loop: it decides whether to search, what to search for, which source to use, whether the results are good enough, and when to stop.

That wins on questions a single retrieval can't answer. Multi-hop questions, where the second search depends on the first answer — 'who manages the team that owns the payments service, and what's their on-call policy?' Multi-source questions that need the document index, a SQL warehouse and a web search. And recovery: if results are poor, reformulate and try again.

The costs are real. Latency and tokens become variable and can grow a lot. Behaviour is non-deterministic, so evaluation and debugging get harder — you have to evaluate trajectories, not just answers. And every tool the agent can call adds security surface.

So I rarely choose between the two outright. The production middle ground is adaptive RAG: a router classifies the query; simple lookups take the fixed, cheap path, and only complex or multi-hop questions enter the loop. The loop has caps from day one — a maximum number of hops, a token budget, a timeout — and a grader that's allowed to abstain."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Fixed pipeline Agentic RAG
retrieval once, fixed order tool calls in a loop
latency / cost predictable variable
multi-hop, multi-source weak strong
evaluation per stage per trajectory

stages.name: Where agentic RAG wins
stages.html: • Second query depends on the first answer; several data sources; iterative refinement after poor results.

stages.name: Where the fixed pipeline wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the cost of the loop (illustrative trace):

Step Action Tokens in Cumulative latency
1 plan + search("payments service owner") 1,200 1.1 s
2 read results, search("team X on-call policy") 3,800 2.6 s
3 grade results, answer 5,200 4.3 s
fixed path, single retrieval answer 2,500 1.4 s

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: does the question need more than one dependent retrieval?
stages.html: • Measure the share of such questions in real traffic; that share is how much of the system should be agentic.

stages.name: What I'd pick

followUps.question: 🧪 Each hop succeeds 90% of the time. What's the success rate of a 4-hop chain?
followUps.html: 0.9⁴ ≈ 66%. Errors compound across hops, which is why caps, graders and evaluation of trajectories matter, and why short chains are preferred.

followUps.question: "Agentic RAG is strictly better."
followUps.html: For single-hop lookups it's slower, costlier and less predictable, with no quality gain. Use it only where the question needs it.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate an agentic retriever?
followUps.html: Final-answer correctness plus trajectory metrics: hops taken, redundant searches, whether the right sources were used, cost and latency per question, and consistency across repeated runs.

followUps.question: How does the router decide?
followUps.html: A small classifier or an LLM call labels query complexity (lookup / multi-hop / aggregation), trained or prompted with examples from real traffic; misroutes are logged and reviewed.

followUps.question: What security concerns does the loop add?
followUps.html: The agent reads untrusted retrieved text and can call tools, so injection can steer it. Keep tools read-only, scope them to the user's permissions, and require approval for anything with side effects (Q37).
