rag-q41.testing: geometry vs task judgement, and why raw similarity thresholds are unreliable.
rag-q41.trap: thresholding on cosine and calling it a relevance filter.
rag-q41.spoken:
"Similarity is geometry: the cosine or dot product between the query vector and a chunk vector from a bi-encoder. It says the two texts are about similar things. It knows nothing about whether the chunk answers this question.

Relevance is a judgement: does this chunk help answer this specific question? A chunk can be highly similar and useless — right topic, wrong year, wrong product, wrong tenant, or it restates the question without answering it.

A cross-encoder reranker or an LLM grader produces something much closer to relevance, because it reads the query and the chunk together.

Two practical consequences. Similarity scores aren't comparable across models or even calibrated within one — 0.8 means different things for different embedders — so never threshold on a raw cosine value as if it were a probability of relevance. And if I need an 'is there any good evidence?' decision, for abstention for example, I base it on reranker or grader scores calibrated against labelled data."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Similarity measures closeness in embedding space; relevance measures whether the text helps answer the question."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
Score Produced by Sees query and chunk together?
similarity bi-encoder cosine / dot no
relevance cross-encoder, LLM grader, human label yes

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Query: "What was the refund window in 2025?"
Chunk A: "Refund window (2023 policy): 14 days."         → very similar, wrong year
Chunk B: "From March 2025, customers have 30 days to…"   → less similar wording, relevant

Threshold on precision of kept chunks recall of relevant chunks

reranker score ≥ calibrated t measure measure

stages.name: Adjacent concept

followUps.question: 🧪 You switch embedding models; top cosine scores drop from ~0.85 to ~0.55. Is retrieval worse?
followUps.html: Not necessarily: different models have different score ranges. Compare recall@k on the golden set; the absolute cosine values mean nothing across models. Any threshold must be re-calibrated.

followUps.question: "Drop chunks with cosine below 0.7 — they're irrelevant."
followUps.html: That's a similarity cut, not a relevance filter, and 0.7 is arbitrary per model. You'll drop relevant chunks and keep similar-but-useless ones.

followUps.question: Why can't a bi-encoder judge relevance well?
followUps.html: It compresses each text independently into one vector; details like dates, negation and which entity are lost before the comparison.

followUps.question: Is a reranker score a probability?
followUps.html: Usually not calibrated; treat it as a score and calibrate a threshold on labelled data if you need a decision.

followUps.question: Where would you surface scores to users?
followUps.html: Rarely raw. Show sources and maybe a qualitative confidence derived from calibrated grader scores; raw cosine numbers mislead users.

rag-q42.testing: a quick screen: nominal length vs storage, and why you'd fuse both.
rag-q42.trap: answering "dense" because dense embeddings feel like the bigger technology.
rag-q42.spoken:
"Sparse, nominally. A sparse vector has one dimension per vocabulary term — tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands — but almost all are zero. A dense vector is short, a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions, and every value is used.

In storage the intuition flips: sparse vectors are stored as term-and-weight pairs for the non-zero entries only, so a chunk's sparse vector is often smaller on disk than its dense one. Learned sparse models like SPLADE sit in between: sparse shape, but with learned expansion terms, so more non-zeros than BM25.

And the reason it matters: they capture different things — exact terms versus meaning — which is why hybrid search fuses both."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.claim: sparse is longer, dense is fuller
stages.html: "Sparse length = vocabulary size (mostly zeros); dense length = model dimension (all used)."

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — bytes per chunk (illustrative):

Dense:   1,024 dims × 4 B                          = 4,096 B
BM25:    ~80 unique terms × (4 B id + 4 B weight)  =   640 B   (nominal length: 50,000+)
SPLADE:  ~250 non-zero terms × 8 B                 = 2,000 B   (nominal length: ~30,000)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
• Nominal length: vocabulary vs model dimension → sparse wins.
  • Stored size: non-zeros × bytes vs dims × bytes → often sparse is smaller.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: quantisation and expansion change the answer
stages.html:
Variant Effect
binary-quantised dense (1,024 bits = 128 B) dense becomes smaller than sparse
long chunks with many unique terms sparse grows
SPLADE expansion sparse with many more non-zeros

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Dense in an ANN index, sparse in an inverted index; fuse with RRF (Q10).

followUps.question: 🧪 Which is faster to search at 10M chunks?
followUps.html: Both are fast with the right index: inverted indexes for sparse (only posting lists of query terms are touched) and ANN graphs for dense. Speed depends on index and query, not on nominal length.

followUps.question: "Dense vectors are longer because they're richer."
followUps.html: Richer per dimension, but far shorter. Richness and length are different things.

followUps.question: What does SPLADE add over BM25?
followUps.html: Learned term weights and expansion (adding related terms not in the text), improving recall on paraphrases while keeping an inverted-index-friendly format.

followUps.question: Why fuse instead of choosing?
followUps.html: Dense handles paraphrase; sparse handles exact identifiers and rare terms. Their failures differ, so fusion covers both (Q55).

followUps.question: Would you move on quickly in an interview?
followUps.html: Yes: one-line answer, the storage twist, then pivot to why you'd use both — that's the part the interviewer actually wants.

dontSay: Stopping at the trivia without the hybrid point.

rag-q43.testing: abstention as a designed feature with triggers, a useful refusal, and a tuned threshold.
rag-q43.trap: treating abstention as failure and forcing an answer out of weak context.
rag-q43.spoken:
"Abstention is a feature, not a failure. A system that answers everything will answer some questions from weak or no evidence, and in RAG that's exactly where confident wrong answers come from.

I'd abstain, or ask a clarifying question, on four triggers. No retrieved chunk passes the relevance bar — measured with a calibrated reranker or grader score, not raw cosine. Sources conflict and metadata can't resolve which applies. The question is out of scope for this assistant. Or the answer can't be supported: every claim must cite a retrieved chunk, and if the draft contains unsupported claims, it doesn't ship.

What the system owes the user instead is a useful refusal: say what it couldn't find — 'I don't see a policy covering refunds for gift cards' — show the nearest things it did find, suggest a narrower question or a clarifying choice, and offer a path to a human or the right team. A bare 'I don't know' feels broken.

The threshold is a product decision with a trade-off: over-refusal reads as a broken product, under-refusal as a lying one. I tune it on the golden set, which includes unanswerable questions, and measure both the answer rate on answerable questions and the abstention rate on unanswerable ones."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: what's the cost of a wrong answer here?
stages.html: • High-stakes (medical, legal, finance, policy) → lean to abstain. Low-stakes → lean to answer with caveats.

stages.name: The triggers
stages.claim: no evidence, conflict, out of scope, unsupported
stages.html:
Trigger Check
no good evidence top rerank/grader score < calibrated threshold
unresolved conflict versions/sources disagree (Q34)
out of scope router/classifier says not our domain
unsupported draft claim-level citation check fails
ambiguity several interpretations with different answers → clarify

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: gate on evidence before and after drafting

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — pick t from a labelled sweep (illustrative numbers):

Threshold t answer rate (answerable) abstention (unanswerable) wrong-answer rate
0.2 97% 40% 9%
0.4 92% 78% 4%
0.6 81% 93% 2%
  • Choose by the cost of a wrong answer vs the cost of a refusal; revisit after any model or index change.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Threshold on raw cosine; refusals with no next step; refusing on missing content without telling content owners; over-refusal after a model swap.

stages.name: What I'd monitor
stages.claim: abstention by topic, and content gaps
stages.html: • Abstention rate by topic and tenant (spikes = ingestion or retrieval problems), user follow-up after refusals, and refused questions clustered into content gaps for owners.

followUps.question: 🧪 Abstention is 30% for questions about a new product launched yesterday. What's going on?
followUps.html: Probably content, not the model: the new product's documents aren't indexed yet (ingestion lag or missing source). The refusals are correct; the fix is freshness and routing the gap to content owners.

followUps.question: "Refusing means the product failed."
followUps.html: A wrong confident answer costs more trust than a clear, helpful refusal. Measured abstention on unanswerable questions is a quality metric.

followUps.question: Why not let the model decide when to abstain?
followUps.html: Models are biased toward answering and poorly calibrated. Use retrieval evidence and claim-level checks outside the model as the gate; model instructions are a backstop.

followUps.question: Clarify or refuse?
followUps.html: Clarify when the question is ambiguous and the options are known (which plan? which region?); refuse when the evidence doesn't exist.

followUps.question: How do refusals improve the corpus?
followUps.html: Cluster refused questions weekly, hand them to content owners as gaps, and track the gap closure rate. Abstention becomes a content roadmap.

rag-q44.testing: locating a recall failure before tuning, and fixing it in cost order.
rag-q44.trap: raising top-k alone — noise goes up, answers get worse.
rag-q44.spoken:
"That's a recall failure: recall of 0.2. Before tuning anything, I'd find where the other eight are lost, because there are four places: the embedding, the index, the filter, and k.

First, the cheap checks. Is a metadata filter excluding them — wrong tenant, date or document-type filter? Are they even in the index — did ingestion or parsing fail for those documents? Then, are they just below the cut-off: retrieve the top 200 and see what rank they sit at.

If they're ranked 20 to 100, it's k and ranking: retrieve more — say 50 — and rerank down to the few that go to the model. If the index is approximate and tuned too tight, raise efSearch and compare against exact search.

If they're nowhere near the top, it's representation. Vocabulary mismatch is the usual cause — the query uses different words, or exact codes and names that dense embeddings blur — so I add BM25 and fuse with RRF. Then the query side: rewriting or multi-query, and decomposition if the question has several parts that no single query covers. Then chunking: if the answer was split across boundaries, no single chunk matches strongly.

I fix in that cost order and re-measure recall@k on the golden set after each change."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "Eight relevant chunks are lost somewhere between ingestion and the top-k cut."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Check How
filter excludes them run the query unfiltered; compare
not indexed look up the chunk IDs in the index
parse failure inspect the stored chunk text
stale embeddings / wrong model version check version stamps

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the rank distribution of missing relevant chunks (illustrative):

Rank bucket in top-200 count Meaning Fix
11–50 5 ranking / k retrieve 50, rerank
51–200 1 weak match hybrid, query rewrite
not found 2 representation / chunking BM25, re-chunk, check ingestion

stages.name: Fix in order
stages.html:
1. Filters and ingestion correctness.
  2. Retrieve more (k 10 → 50), rerank to 5; raise efSearch if ANN recall vs exact is low.
  3. Add BM25 + RRF for vocabulary/ID mismatch.
  4. Query rewriting / multi-query / decomposition.
  5. Re-chunk (structure-aware, small-to-big, contextual chunking).

stages.name: Validate
stages.html: • Recall@50 and recall@5 after rerank on the golden set; end-to-end faithfulness to confirm the extra recall reaches the answer.

followUps.question: 🧪 You raise top-k from 10 to 40 and send all 40 to the LLM. Recall improves; answers get worse. Why?
followUps.html: More evidence is retrieved, but the prompt now has 30 more weak chunks: dilution, lost in the middle, conflicts and cost. Retrieve 40, rerank, send 5.

followUps.question: "Just increase k."
followUps.html: It helps only the chunks ranked just below the cut, and without reranking it adds noise to the prompt. Locate the loss first.

followUps.question: How do you know if ANN approximation is the problem?
followUps.html: Run exact (brute-force) search for the same queries; if exact finds the chunks and ANN doesn't, raise efSearch/nprobe or revisit index parameters.

followUps.question: Why might relevant chunks never match?
followUps.html: Different vocabulary (jargon vs plain words), identifiers blurred by the embedder, missing context in the chunk (lost subject), or the answer spread across chunks.

followUps.question: How do you prevent recall regressions?
followUps.html: Recall@k on the golden set in CI for every chunking, embedding, index or filter change; production sampling of queries with low top scores; alerts on empty-result spikes.

rag-q45.testing: that chunking and embedding are one coupled, versioned decision.
rag-q45.trap: tuning chunk size against a fixed model, or swapping models without re-chunking.
rag-q45.spoken:
"They're one decision, not two.

The embedding model sets hard and soft limits. The hard limit is its maximum input length: past it, text is silently truncated, so part of every oversized chunk is invisible to dense search. The soft limit is what it was trained on: many retrieval models were trained on passages of a few hundred tokens, so very long chunks produce blurrier vectors even under the maximum. Asymmetric retrieval models handle longer passages better than symmetric sentence models. Long-context embedding models allow late chunking, which loosens the coupling.

The documents set the other side: how long a self-contained unit is — a clause, a FAQ answer, a section — and whether there's structure to split on.

So I pick the pair together on the golden set: two or three embedding candidates crossed with two or three chunking schemes, measured on recall@k and end-to-end faithfulness, plus storage and cost.

And I version them together. The embedding model, chunk scheme, index and prompt are one contract: change the model, and I re-chunk if the optimal size moved, re-embed, and re-evaluate."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html: "Chunk size must fit both the model's effective input range and the document's natural answer units."

stages.name: What the model constrains
stages.claim: max length and training regime set the ceiling
stages.html:
Property Effect on chunking
max input tokens hard ceiling (silent truncation beyond)
training passage length soft optimum
asymmetric training tolerates longer passages
long-context + late chunking chunk after encoding; context preserved

stages.name: What the documents constrain
stages.claim: the natural answer unit sets the floor
stages.html: • Self-contained unit size (clause, FAQ, section), structure markers, tables.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: which pair wins on your golden set?
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the grid to run (cells to measure):

Embedder \ Chunking 256 recursive 512 recursive sections (structure-aware)
model A (512 max) measure measure truncation risk: check
model B (8k max) measure measure measure
model B + late chunking measure measure measure

stages.name: How I'd pick the pair
stages.html: • Choose the best recall/faithfulness per cost; stamp the pair as one contract version; any change → re-index + re-eval (Q31).

followUps.question: 🧪 Model max length 512 tokens; section-based chunks average 900. What do you do?
followUps.html: Either split sections into sub-chunks under 512 with small-to-big (match sub-chunk, send section), or choose a longer-context embedder. Don't leave 43% of each section silently unembedded.

followUps.question: "Chunk size is independent of the model."
followUps.html: The model's input limit and training regime directly determine what chunk sizes embed well. They move together.

followUps.question: Why do long chunks blur?
followUps.html: The embedding pools information from all tokens into one vector; more topics in the chunk means the vector sits between them and matches each less strongly.

followUps.question: What does late chunking change?
followUps.html: The document is encoded in full context, then pooled per chunk, so small chunks keep document context; chunk size can shrink without losing meaning (Q11).

followUps.question: How often would you revisit the pair?
followUps.html: On model upgrades, new document types, or eval failures pointing at truncation or lost context. It's a planned migration each time, not a tweak.

rag-q46.testing: an honest account of extraction, entity resolution, schema and incremental updates.
rag-q46.trap: pitching GraphRAG's benefits with no account of build and maintenance cost.
rag-q46.spoken:
"If I haven't built one in production, I'd say so and describe the costs as I understand them; if I have, I'd anchor on real numbers. Either way, the costs fall in four places.

Extraction: an LLM call per chunk to pull entities and relationships, over the whole corpus, often with a second pass for quality. That's the biggest direct bill and it recurs for new content.

Entity resolution: 'J. Smith', 'John Smith' and 'Smith, J.' must become one node, and two different John Smiths must not. It needs normalisation, embeddings or string similarity, and rules or human review for ambiguous cases. Errors here corrupt every traversal.

Schema: open extraction is flexible but produces a messy graph with many near-duplicate relation types; a fixed ontology is clean but misses things and needs maintenance as the domain changes.

Incremental updates: a new document can merge entities that were separate, change relationships, and invalidate community summaries, so updates aren't simple appends.

Quality work is unbounded, so I scope it: only the entity and relation types the questions actually need, measured against a set of relational questions, with the graph used alongside vector retrieval rather than instead of it."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "A knowledge graph for RAG is built by extracting entities and relations from text, resolving duplicates, and storing them for traversal."

stages.name: Where the cost goes
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the build bill (illustrative):

200k chunks × (600 chunk + 800 prompt) tokens = 280M input tokens (+ output) for extraction
Second-pass verification on 20%              = +56M tokens
Entity resolution: ~1.5M raw mentions → ~300k entities after merge (review queue for low-confidence merges)
Community summaries (GraphRAG): one LLM call per community per level, recomputed when communities change
Cost centre Recurring?
extraction yes, per new/changed chunk
entity resolution yes, and can re-merge existing nodes
schema maintenance yes, as the domain evolves
summaries yes, on community changes
second store ops yes

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
• Wrong merges (two people become one) → wrong answers with confident paths.
  • Missed merges → fragmented graph, traversals miss links.
  • Relation-type sprawl in open extraction.
  • Stale summaries after updates.

stages.name: How I'd scope it
stages.claim: only the entity types the questions need
stages.html: • Start from the relational questions users ask; extract only the needed types; fixed ontology for those; measure path accuracy and answer quality against hybrid vector RAG on those questions.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Vector search finds entry entities; the graph expands 1–2 hops; most of the benefit with a smaller graph (Q20).

followUps.question: 🧪 A new press release mentions "J. Smith (CFO)". Your graph has two John Smiths. What must happen?
followUps.html: Entity resolution decides which node it is (role, company, context) or creates a new one; a wrong merge changes existing relationship paths. That's why updates can touch existing parts of the graph, not just add nodes.

followUps.question: "The LLM builds the graph automatically, so it's cheap."
followUps.html: Extraction is automated but expensive at corpus scale, and resolution, schema and updates need ongoing engineering and review. The ongoing cost is the real cost.

followUps.question: Open extraction or fixed ontology?
followUps.html: Fixed ontology for production questions you know; open extraction for exploration. Many teams start open, then consolidate into a schema.

followUps.question: How do you measure graph quality?
followUps.html: Precision/recall of extracted relations on a labelled sample, merge accuracy on a labelled set of mentions, and end-to-end accuracy on relational questions.

followUps.question: When would you stop investing?
followUps.html: When hybrid vector RAG answers the relational questions nearly as well at a fraction of the cost, or the relational question share is small. Decide with the eval, not enthusiasm.

dontSay: Claiming production experience you don't have.

rag-q47.testing: structure-preserving ingestion, clause-level chunks and citations, cross-references, versions and abstention.
rag-q47.trap: fixed-size chunking a contract — severing the clause from the definition it depends on.
rag-q47.spoken:
"Legal documents are defined by structure, so the design preserves structure end to end.

Ingestion: layout-aware parsing, not text dumps, so the section hierarchy — article, section, clause, sub-clause — numbering, defined terms and tables survive. Scanned documents need OCR with quality checks. Every document gets metadata: type, parties, jurisdiction, effective date, version and status — draft, executed, superseded.

Chunking follows the structure: one chunk per clause or sub-clause, with the full section path attached — 'MSA › 9 Liability › 9.2 Cap' — and the document title prepended for embedding. Tables are extracted as separate chunks with their caption and header row, so numbers keep their meaning.

Cross-references and definitions need special handling. 'As defined in Section 1.4' or a capitalised defined term means the clause alone isn't enough. At indexing time I resolve references into links, and at retrieval time I pull in the referenced definitions and clauses alongside the hit — a small graph of references, not a full knowledge graph.

Retrieval is hybrid: BM25 matters for exact terms and section numbers, dense for paraphrase, then a reranker. Filters for document, version, jurisdiction and effective date are mandatory.

Generation must cite at clause level — every statement points to a section number — and abstain rather than guess. For high-stakes use, a lawyer reviews, and the UI shows the clause text beside the answer."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Users: lawyers vs business users. Questions: "what's our liability cap with X?", "which contracts have auto-renewal?", "compare indemnity across vendors". Stakes: high → citations and abstention mandatory.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.claim: millions of clause chunks, many versions
stages.html:
20k contracts × 40 pages ≈ 800k pages → ~2–3M clause-level chunks (illustrative)
Versions: drafts + executed + amendments → version and status filters required
Questions across contracts (aggregation) → structured extraction into a table, not retrieval alone

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: structure preserved from parse to citation

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — resolving references into the retrieved context:

import re
clauses = {"9.2": "Liability is capped at the Fees paid in the prior 12 months, except as in Section 9.4.",
           "9.4": "The cap does not apply to breaches of Clause 11 (Confidentiality).",
           "1.7": '"Fees" means the amounts payable under Schedule 2.'}
def expand(cid):
    refs = re.findall(r"Section (\d+\.\d+)", clauses[cid])
    terms = ["1.7"] if "Fees" in clauses[cid] else []
    return [cid] + refs + terms
print(expand("9.2"))
# → ['9.2', '9.4', '1.7']

The hit on 9.2 brings its exception (9.4) and the definition of "Fees" (1.7) into context, so the answer isn't missing the carve-out.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Guard
fixed-size chunks sever exceptions clause-level chunks + reference expansion
tables flattened table extraction with headers
draft vs executed confusion status/version filters, default to executed
cross-contract questions answered from top-k structured extraction (e.g. "renewal term" per contract) into a table + SQL
uncited answers claim-level citation check; abstain otherwise

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html: • Clause classification (indemnity, liability, termination) as metadata; structured fields extracted per contract for portfolio queries; lawyer feedback loop into the golden set.

followUps.question: 🧪 "Which of our vendor contracts auto-renew?" Why is top-k retrieval the wrong tool?
followUps.html: It's an aggregation over all contracts; top-k returns a handful. Extract a structured "auto-renewal: yes/no, term" field per contract at ingestion and answer with a query, with links to each clause.

followUps.question: "Fixed 512-token chunks are fine for contracts."
followUps.html: They split clauses from their exceptions and definitions, so answers miss carve-outs — the most dangerous error in legal work. Chunk by clause.

followUps.question: Why does BM25 matter here?
followUps.html: Section numbers, defined terms, party names and legal phrases need exact matching; dense retrieval blurs them.

followUps.question: How do you handle amendments?
followUps.html: Link amendments to the clauses they modify, mark superseded text, and present the current consolidated clause with a note of the amendment; filter by effective date for "as of" questions.

followUps.question: Who is accountable for answers?
followUps.html: The system is decision support: answers cite clauses, the UI shows source text, and high-stakes conclusions go to a lawyer. Logs keep the question, retrieved clauses and answer for audit.

rag-q48.testing: a crisp, architectural answer: freshness, provenance, permissions — at scale.
rag-q48.trap: "it reduces hallucination" as the whole answer.
rag-q48.spoken: "RAG attaches an external, swappable knowledge store to a frozen model. That gives three things neither a bigger prompt nor a better model can: freshness — update a document and the answer changes in minutes, no retraining; provenance — every answer can cite the passage it came from, so people can verify it; and permissions — each user only retrieves what they're allowed to see, enforced outside the model. And it does that at a corpus size no context window holds, at a per-query cost of a few thousand tokens."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: a swappable knowledge store for a frozen model
stages.html: "RAG separates what the system knows (an index) from how it reasons (the model)."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
Property Why a bigger prompt / better model can't give it
freshness model knowledge is frozen at training; prompts must be rebuilt by someone
provenance parametric knowledge can't point to a source
permissions the model can't enforce who may see what
scale millions of documents don't fit any window
cost a few thousand tokens per query vs the whole corpus

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: the problem moves into data engineering
stages.html:
• Retrieval misses, bad parsing, stale indexes — RAG shifts problems to data engineering.

💻 Prove it — the per-query token comparison (illustrative):

Corpus 50k documents ≈ 100M tokens → cannot be "a bigger prompt"
RAG query: 5 chunks × 400 + 600 prompt ≈ 2,600 tokens

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.html: • Policy and support assistants where answers must cite and update daily; per-tenant document search.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Small stable corpora, pure reasoning tasks, or aggregation questions (Q49).

followUps.question: 🧪 A policy changed an hour ago. What does each option need to reflect it?
followUps.html: RAG: re-index the document (minutes). Fine-tuned model: a new training run. Bigger prompt: someone must update the stuffed text in every prompt. Better model: nothing — it doesn't know.

followUps.question: "RAG exists to stop hallucination."
followUps.html: It helps factuality when retrieval succeeds, but its structural benefits are freshness, provenance and permissions. Hallucination still needs grounding checks (Q18).

followUps.question: Is RAG only for LLM chat?
followUps.html: No: the same pattern powers search with generated summaries, agents' knowledge tools, and extraction pipelines needing reference data.

followUps.question: What does RAG cost you?
followUps.html: A data pipeline to run (ingestion, freshness, permissions), retrieval latency, and evaluation work for two problems instead of one.

followUps.question: How would you pitch it to a CFO?
followUps.html: Answers that stay current without retraining, can be audited to a source, and respect access rules — at a predictable per-query cost.

dontSay: "It gives the model more knowledge" without the mechanism.

rag-q49.testing: knowing when RAG is the wrong tool, with the right alternative for each case.
rag-q49.trap: "RAG is always the answer for enterprise AI."
rag-q49.spoken:
"Three situations.

First, there's no retrievable knowledge. The task is reasoning, writing, transformation or classification, where the model needs instructions and examples, not documents — rewriting emails in a brand voice, classifying tickets into ten categories. RAG adds a pipeline and latency for nothing; a prompt, or a fine-tune for behaviour, is the tool.

Second, the corpus fits comfortably in context and rarely changes: a 30-page handbook, one product manual. Put it in the prompt, use prompt caching so the repeated prefix is cheap, and skip chunking, embedding and index operations entirely. Revisit if it grows or needs permissions.

Third, the questions need the whole corpus or exact computation: 'how many contracts expire this quarter', 'total refunds by region', 'what are the main themes across all feedback'. Top-k retrieval returns a handful of chunks and the model will confidently summarise or 'sum' them wrongly. That's SQL over structured data, a structured extraction step at ingestion, or a map-reduce over everything.

The honest meta-point: RAG shifts the problem into data engineering — parsing, freshness, permissions, evaluation — so it should earn that cost."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: does the task need to look things up?
stages.html: "RAG is for answering from a large, changing, permissioned body of text; outside that, it's overhead."

stages.name: No retrievable knowledge
stages.html: • Style transfer, classification, extraction from the input itself, pure reasoning.

stages.name: The corpus fits in context
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — a small stable corpus (illustrative):

Handbook: 30 pages ≈ 15k tokens, changes quarterly, 300 queries/day
Full context + prompt caching: 15k cached prefix tokens per call, no pipeline to run
RAG: chunking, embeddings, index, freshness jobs, eval for retrieval — for 15k tokens of text

stages.name: Whole-corpus or exact questions
stages.html:
Question Tool
counts, sums, filters over records SQL / structured extraction
"themes across all documents" clustering / map-reduce summarisation
"compare all contracts on X" per-document extraction into a table

stages.name: What I'd recommend instead
stages.claim: the simplest tool that passes the eval
stages.html: • Build the golden set first; try prompt-only or full-context; add RAG only when it measurably wins.

followUps.question: 🧪 "Summarise the top complaints across 20,000 reviews." RAG or not?
followUps.html: Not top-k RAG: the answer needs all reviews. Cluster embeddings or run a map-reduce summarisation over batches, then summarise the clusters with counts.

followUps.question: "Every enterprise AI app needs RAG."
followUps.html: Only those answering from large, changing, permissioned knowledge. Many valuable apps are prompt-only, structured-data or workflow automation.

followUps.question: What would make you switch the small-corpus case to RAG?
followUps.html: Growth beyond comfortable context size, per-user permissions, frequent updates, or cost/latency of the full context becoming a problem.

followUps.question: How do you have that conversation with a team excited about RAG?
followUps.html: Show the golden-set results of the simpler option and the operational cost of the pipeline; agree on the metric that would justify RAG.

followUps.question: What's the risk of building RAG unnecessarily?
followUps.html: An extra system to run (ingestion, freshness, permissions), more failure modes, higher latency and a false sense of "grounded" answers — with no quality gain.

links.label: Text to SQL & Structured Data RAG

rag-q50.testing: that text extraction flattens tables, retrieval still "passes", and the fix is upstream.
rag-q50.trap: blaming the model or tuning retrieval.
rag-q50.spoken:
"The extractor flattened the table. Plain PDF text extraction reads text in drawing order, so a table becomes a stream of numbers and labels with the row-and-column structure gone — sometimes with columns interleaved, headers separated from values, or a table split across pages without its header.

Retrieval still 'works': the chunk contains the right keywords — 'Pro plan', 'price', '49' — so it embeds as relevant and ranks well. Then the model receives a jumble like 'Plan Basic Pro Price 19 49 Seats 5 20' and has to guess which number belongs to which row and column. It guesses fluently and confidently, and often wrongly.

To confirm, I look at the stored chunk text for a failing question — the evidence is usually obvious — and I slice the golden set by answer type: table questions failing while prose questions pass is the signature.

The fix is at parse time: layout-aware parsing or table-structure extraction that outputs tables as Markdown or HTML with headers; each table stored as its own chunk with its caption and header row, and large tables split by rows with the header repeated; plus a short text description of what the table contains, to help retrieval. For scanned or complex tables, vision-based parsers."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "The table's meaning lives in its grid; plain text extraction keeps the tokens and loses the grid."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: missing OCR or the wrong table retrieved
stages.html:
• Is the table even in the index (image-only tables without OCR)?
  • Is the right table retrieved, or a similar table from another document/year?
  • Is the question arithmetic over the table (then the model needs a tool, not just context)?

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — flattened vs structured:

Flattened (plain extraction):
  Plan Basic Pro Enterprise Price/month 19 49 Custom Seats 5 20 Unlimited
Structured (layout-aware → Markdown):
  | Plan       | Price/month | Seats     |
  |------------|-------------|-----------|
  | Basic      | 19          | 5         |
  | Pro        | 49          | 20        |
  | Enterprise | Custom      | Unlimited |
Question: "How many seats does Pro include?" → flattened: guess; structured: 20

stages.name: Fix at parse time
stages.claim: tables as structured chunks with headers
stages.html:
Step Detail
layout-aware parser detect tables; output Markdown/HTML with headers
table as its own chunk caption + header row + rows; section path metadata
big tables split by rows, repeat header in each chunk
table summary text "Pricing by plan: price per month and seats" for retrieval
scanned / complex vision-language or specialised table models

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: a table-question slice in the golden set
stages.html: • A table-question slice in the golden set; accuracy before/after; spot-check parsed tables against the PDF.

followUps.question: 🧪 A table spans two pages; page 2 has no header. What does the model see for rows on page 2?
followUps.html: Numbers without column names, possibly in a separate chunk. It will guess which column each value is. Fix: stitch multi-page tables and repeat headers per chunk.

followUps.question: "Use a stronger model; it'll figure out the table."
followUps.html: The structure is gone before the model sees it; a stronger model guesses more fluently, not more correctly. Fix the parse.

followUps.question: Why does retrieval still succeed?
followUps.html: The chunk contains the right terms, so similarity is high. Retrieval quality metrics look fine while answers fail — which is why you evaluate end to end by slice.

followUps.question: What about numeric questions over tables?
followUps.html: For sums or comparisons, extract tables into structured storage and compute with code/SQL rather than asking the model to do arithmetic over text.

followUps.question: How do you catch this before users do?
followUps.html: A golden-set slice for tables per document type, a parser quality check in the ingestion pipeline (e.g. table detection counts vs expected), and sampled visual QA of parsed output for new document sources.

dontSay: Tuning retrieval for a parsing problem.
Tables chunked with surrounding prose by size.

rag-q51.testing: tying parser choice to where meaning lives, and to what it enables downstream.
rag-q51.trap: one parser for every document type.
rag-q51.spoken:
"Layout-aware parsing pays off exactly when meaning lives in structure rather than in running text.

Plain text extraction is fast and cheap, and fine for documents that are essentially prose in a single column: articles, emails, simple policies, HTML pages converted to text.

Layout parsing earns its cost when the document has tables, where the grid is the meaning; heading hierarchies, where knowing which section a paragraph belongs to matters; multi-column layouts, where plain extraction interleaves columns; forms with key-value fields; figures and charts with captions; headers, footers and page numbers that pollute text; and scanned pages that need OCR.

It also enables the downstream steps: structure-aware chunking needs headings; clause-level citations need section numbers; table chunks need table structure. Without layout, those are impossible.

The cost is real — slower ingestion, GPU or API spend for vision models, and more failure modes to monitor — so I choose per document type: detect the type at ingestion, route prose to cheap extraction and structured or scanned documents to layout-aware parsing, and measure the table and section slices of the golden set to prove the spend is worth it."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: cost of parsing vs cost of lost structure
stages.html: "Pay for layout parsing where the structure carries the answer."

stages.name: Where plain extraction is enough
stages.html: • Single-column prose, HTML articles, emails, plain policies.

stages.name: Where layout parsing earns it
stages.claim: tables, headings, columns, forms and scans
stages.html:
Document feature What plain extraction breaks
tables row/column meaning
heading hierarchy section context, structure-aware chunks
multi-column interleaved sentences
forms key–value pairing
headers/footers noise in every chunk
scans no text at all without OCR

💻 Prove it — per-type routing and its evidence (cells to measure):

Doc type Parser table/section Q accuracy ingest cost per 1k pages

stages.name: What I'd do
stages.html: • Classify documents at ingestion (born-digital vs scanned, table density, columns); route to the cheapest parser that preserves the needed structure; keep parsed output (Markdown/JSON) so re-chunking doesn't require re-parsing.

followUps.question: 🧪 A two-column research paper parsed as plain text. What do chunks look like?
followUps.html: Lines from the left and right columns alternate, so sentences are spliced mid-way. Embeddings become noisy and answers quote nonsense. Layout parsing reads each column in order.

followUps.question: "Use the best vision parser on everything."
followUps.html: Expensive and slow on prose where plain extraction is equally good. Route by document type.

followUps.question: Why store parsed output?
followUps.html: Parsing is the slowest ingestion step; storing Markdown/JSON lets you re-chunk or re-embed without re-parsing when the pipeline changes.

followUps.question: How do you check parser quality?
followUps.html: Sampled visual comparisons of parsed output vs the original, table-detection counts, and the table/section slices of the golden set.

followUps.question: Build or buy parsing?
followUps.html: Buy or use strong open-source parsers for common formats; build routing, quality checks and document-type-specific fixes. Parsing quality is a big share of RAG quality, so evaluate vendors on your documents.

dontSay: Parsing choices without a table/section eval slice.

rag-q52.testing: the averaging effect of one vector per document, and the generation-side cost.
rag-q52.trap: "because of the token limit" as the only reason.
rag-q52.spoken:
"If you embed a 40-page document as one vector, retrieval gets much worse for specific questions, and generation gets expensive.

One vector has to represent everything in the document, so it lands somewhere between all its topics. A question about one clause on page 27 is similar to a small part of the document, but the averaged vector is dominated by everything else, so the match is weak and another document may outrank it. Many embedding models would also truncate the input long before 40 pages.

And even if retrieval found the right document, you'd send the whole thing to the LLM: expensive, slow, and the relevant clause lost in the middle.

Chunking makes each vector mean one thing sharply and lets the model receive the passages that matter. Whole-document embeddings still have a place — for routing or document-level search, like finding which contract to look in — often combined with chunk retrieval inside the chosen document."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html: "One vector per document blurs specific content; one document per answer bloats the prompt."

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — a document vector as the mean of its topic vectors:

import numpy as np
topics = np.eye(8)                          # 8 unrelated topics, one direction each
doc = topics.mean(axis=0); doc /= np.linalg.norm(doc)
query = topics[5]                            # a question about topic 5
chunk = topics[5]                            # the chunk that covers topic 5
print(round(float(query @ doc), 3), round(float(query @ chunk), 3))
# → 0.354 1.0

The whole-document vector matches the question at 0.35; the right chunk matches at 1.0. Real documents are less extreme, but the direction of the effect is the same.

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: more topics per vector, weaker match to each
stages.html:
• The more topics in the text, the weaker its similarity to any single-topic question.
  • Generation cost scales with what you send.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Case Whole-document embedding works
short, single-topic docs (FAQ entries, product cards) ✅ doc = chunk
document routing ("which contract?") ✅ then chunk-level search inside
late chunking chunks get document context without averaging it away

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Document-level retrieval (summary or title embeddings) to narrow scope, chunk-level retrieval within, parents for context (Q14).

followUps.question: 🧪 A 3-sentence FAQ answer: chunk it further?
followUps.html: No: it's already one topic and one answer. Splitting it would separate the question from its answer. Chunk size follows the document's natural unit.

followUps.question: "We chunk only because of the model's token limit."
followUps.html: The limit is one reason, but even long-context embedders produce blurrier vectors for multi-topic text, and generation cost/quality suffers with whole documents.

followUps.question: Why do FAQs work well without chunking?
followUps.html: Each entry is short and single-topic, so the whole entry is already a sharp unit.

followUps.question: Is there a document-level vector worth keeping?
followUps.html: Yes, for routing, deduplication and "similar documents" features — alongside chunk vectors.

followUps.question: How does this change with long-context LLMs?
followUps.html: You can send more text per answer, so parents can be larger, but retrieval still needs sharp units to find the right place. Chunk for matching; send generously if the budget allows.

dontSay: One vector per 40-page document for Q&A.

rag-q53.testing: contrastive training as the reason angles track relatedness.
rag-q53.trap: "geometry is magic" — cosine means something only because training made it so.
rag-q53.spoken:
"Mechanically, an embedding model is usually a transformer encoder. Text goes in as tokens, the encoder produces a vector per token, and those are pooled — averaged, or taken from a special token — into one fixed-length vector, often normalised to unit length.

Cosine similarity between two such vectors is meaningful because the model was trained to make it meaningful. Retrieval embedders are trained contrastively: given pairs that should match — a question and its answer passage, a title and its article — the loss pushes their vectors to have a high dot product, and pushes non-matching texts in the same batch, and deliberately chosen hard negatives, apart. After enough of that, the direction of a vector encodes what the text is about, and the angle between two vectors reflects how related the model learned them to be.

Two consequences follow. Similarity reflects the training objective: a model trained on paraphrases scores paraphrases high, and a model trained on question–answer pairs scores questions near their answers. And the numbers aren't universal: scores aren't comparable across models, and there's no fixed threshold that means 'relevant'.

Also, 'related' isn't 'correct': an embedding can't tell a statement from its negation reliably, or 2023 from 2025 — which is why rerankers and metadata filters exist."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: a learned projection where angle tracks relatedness
stages.html: "An embedding is an encoder's pooled output, trained contrastively so matching texts point in similar directions."

stages.name: How it works
stages.html: • Training: InfoNCE-style loss over (query, positive) pairs with in-batch and hard negatives.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import numpy as np
emb = {"refund policy": [0.9, 0.1, 0.2], "return an item for money back": [0.85, 0.15, 0.25], "GPU kernel fusion": [0.05, 0.95, 0.1]}
V = {k: np.array(v) / np.linalg.norm(v) for k, v in emb.items()}
q = V["refund policy"]
for k, v in V.items(): print(f"{float(q @ v):.3f}  {k}")
# → 1.000  refund policy
# → 0.996  return an item for money back
# → 0.180  GPU kernel fusion

Toy 3-D vectors chosen by hand to show the arithmetic; a trained model produces this pattern for real text because the loss pushed it there.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Limitation Example
negation and numbers blur "covered" vs "not covered"
entity/date confusion 2023 vs 2025 policy
domain shift jargon unseen in training
model-specific score ranges no universal threshold

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: candidates from embeddings, decisions from rerankers
stages.html: • Use embeddings for candidate generation; rerank for relevance; metadata filters for dates/entities; evaluate on your data.

followUps.question: 🧪 Vectors are L2-normalised. Is dot product the same as cosine similarity?
followUps.html: Yes: cosine = a·b / (|a||b|), and with |a| = |b| = 1 it's just a·b. That's why many indexes use inner product on normalised vectors.

followUps.question: "Cosine similarity measures meaning."
followUps.html: It measures whatever relatedness the training objective taught. Change the training data and the same pair gets a different score.

followUps.question: What are hard negatives?
followUps.html: Passages that look relevant but aren't (same topic, wrong answer). Training on them teaches finer distinctions than random negatives.

followUps.question: Why normalise?
followUps.html: So vector length doesn't affect similarity (longer texts don't dominate), and so dot product equals cosine for efficient search.

followUps.question: When would you fine-tune an embedder?
followUps.html: When your notion of relevance differs from the general training data (internal jargon, legal distinctions), with mined or synthetic query–positive pairs and hard negatives, measured on your golden set.

dontSay: Using embeddings to distinguish dates or negation.

rag-q54.testing: fewer dimensions, fewer bytes, and protecting recall with rescoring.
rag-q54.trap: quantising without measuring recall, or without a rescoring step.
rag-q54.spoken:
"Memory is vectors times dimensions times bytes per value, plus index overhead, so I attack each factor and protect recall with a rescoring step.

Fewer dimensions: Matryoshka-trained models let me truncate vectors — 1,024 down to 256, for example — with a modest recall loss, measured on my golden set.

Fewer bytes: int8 scalar quantisation cuts memory four times with a small recall loss; binary quantisation keeps one bit per dimension, a 32-times cut, with a large loss on its own.

Protect recall with two-stage search: search the compressed index for a shortlist — say the top 100 — then rescore that shortlist with full-precision vectors kept on disk or in cheaper storage, and return the top 10. The compressed index only has to get the right answers into the shortlist, which it does far better than getting them into the top 10.

Also: product quantisation in IVF-PQ for very large indexes; disk-based indexes like DiskANN; and removing waste — duplicate chunks, superseded versions and boilerplate like headers and footers that shouldn't be indexed at all.

Every step is measured: recall@10 against the uncompressed baseline on the golden set, and p95 latency."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • RAM for in-memory indexes vs disk; replicas multiply it; index overhead (HNSW graph).

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
50M chunks × 1,024 dims × 4 B (float32)      = 205 GB   (× replicas)
Matryoshka 256 dims, float32                 =  51 GB
int8, 1,024 dims                             =  51 GB
binary, 1,024 dims                           = 6.4 GB   (+ float vectors on disk for rescoring)

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — binary search + float rescoring (clustered synthetic data, NumPy):

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n, d = 20_000, 256
centers = rng.normal(size=(400, d)); X = centers[rng.integers(0, 400, n)] + 0.6 * rng.normal(size=(n, d))
X = (X / np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)).astype(np.float32)
Q = X[rng.integers(0, n, 100)] + 0.05 * rng.normal(size=(100, d)).astype(np.float32)
truth = np.argsort(-(Q @ X.T), axis=1)[:, :10]
B, QB = np.packbits(X > 0, axis=1), np.packbits(Q > 0, axis=1)
ham = np.unpackbits(QB[:, None, :] ^ B[None, :, :], axis=2).sum(2)
recall = lambda got: np.mean([len(set(a) & set(b)) / 10 for a, b in zip(got, truth)])
short = np.argsort(ham, axis=1)[:, :100]
res = np.array([s[np.argsort(-(X[s] @ q))[:10]] for s, q in zip(short, Q)])
print(d * 4, "->", d // 8, "bytes | binary recall@10", round(recall(short[:, :10]), 2), "| + rescore", round(recall(res), 2))
# → 1024 -> 32 bytes | binary recall@10 0.46 | + rescore 1.0

Binary alone keeps under half of the true top-10; rescoring a 100-item binary shortlist with float vectors recovers all of them here. Real embeddings behave similarly in direction; measure on yours.

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Lever Saving Recall protection
Matryoshka truncation 2–4× rescore with full dims
int8 scalar quantisation 4× usually small loss; rescore if needed
binary quantisation 32× shortlist + float rescore
PQ (IVF-PQ) 10–60× rescore shortlist
DiskANN / disk tiers RAM → SSD tuned for high recall
remove duplicates, boilerplate, superseded varies improves quality too

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Quantising a model not trained for it (large loss); no rescoring; truncating a non-Matryoshka model; forgetting replicas in the cost model.

stages.name: What I'd monitor
stages.html: • Recall@10 vs a float baseline on periodic golden-set runs, p95 latency, memory per shard, shortlist size vs recall.

followUps.question: 🧪 You truncate a non-Matryoshka model's 1,024-dim vectors to 256. What happens?
followUps.html: Recall can drop sharply: its information isn't concentrated in the first dimensions. Truncation only works well with models trained for it; otherwise use PCA or quantisation, and measure.

followUps.question: "Binary quantisation ruins recall."
followUps.html: On its own it loses a lot, but as a first stage with float rescoring of a shortlist, recall can be close to the baseline at a fraction of the memory.

followUps.question: Why does rescoring work so well?
followUps.html: The compressed search only needs to place true neighbours somewhere in the top-100, which is much easier than ranking them exactly; float vectors then order the shortlist precisely.

followUps.question: Where do the float vectors live?
followUps.html: On SSD or in object storage/a cheaper store keyed by chunk ID; only 100 are read per query, so latency stays low.

followUps.question: How do you present the savings?
followUps.html: A table of memory, cost, recall@10 and p95 for each option on the golden set, with the chosen configuration and its measured recall loss.

rag-q55.testing: paraphrase vs exact tokens, with concrete losing classes.
rag-q55.trap: "dense retrieval is strictly better than BM25."
rag-q55.spoken:
"Dense retrieval matches meaning. It's excellent when the query and the document use different words for the same thing — 'how do I get my money back' finding a section titled 'Refund policy' — and on natural-language questions, synonyms and cross-lingual matching with multilingual models.

It reliably loses to keyword search in two classes.

Exact identifiers: product codes, part numbers, error codes, ticket IDs, version strings, function names. 'Error E4471' — the embedding sees a fragment of tokens with little meaning, and a document about error E4472 looks almost identical. BM25 matches the exact string.

Rare or new terms the embedding model didn't learn: new product names, internal project codenames, fresh jargon, uncommon surnames. The model maps them to something vaguely similar; BM25 treats a rare term as highly informative, which is exactly right.

A third, softer class: queries that must match an exact phrase or quote.

That's why hybrid search exists: run both and fuse ranks, and for identifier-heavy corpora even route ID-looking queries to keyword first."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html: "Dense retrieval generalises across wording; keyword retrieval rewards exact, rare tokens."

stages.name: Where dense wins
stages.html: • Paraphrase, synonyms, conversational questions, cross-lingual queries, typo tolerance.

stages.name: Where keyword wins
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the losing classes (illustrative):

Query Dense behaviour BM25 behaviour
"error E4471 on sync" returns general sync-error pages, maybe E4472 exact page with E4471
"PRJ-ORCA rollout date" (internal codename) vague matches to "rollout" exact codename hits
"SKU 88-1020-B dimensions" similar SKUs exact SKU
"how do I get my money back" refund policy ✅ weak (no shared words)

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: do users search with exact strings?
stages.html: • Mine query logs for IDs, codes, codenames; measure dense vs BM25 recall on that slice (Q23).

stages.name: What I'd build
stages.claim: hybrid with RRF, routing for IDs
stages.html: • Dense + BM25 fused with RRF, reranked; regex/classifier routes pure-ID queries to keyword first.

followUps.question: 🧪 Why would "E4471" and "E4472" embed almost identically?
followUps.html: They tokenize into mostly the same pieces and carry little learned meaning, so the pooled vectors are close. The one-digit difference that matters to the user barely moves the embedding.

followUps.question: "Modern embeddings handle IDs fine."
followUps.html: They handle common entities; arbitrary codes and new names are exactly where they fail. Measure on your identifier slice.

followUps.question: Why does BM25 favour rare terms?
followUps.html: Inverse document frequency: a term in few documents gets a high weight, so an exact match on a rare code dominates the score.

followUps.question: Can fine-tuning fix dense on IDs?
followUps.html: Partly, for recurring vocabulary, but new identifiers keep appearing. Keyword search handles them without retraining.

followUps.question: What does this imply for evaluation?
followUps.html: Slice the golden set by query class (natural language vs identifier vs rare term); averages hide the class where dense fails.

rag-q56.testing: routing by intent, cheap-first with escalation, and logging misroutes.
rag-q56.trap: an LLM call for every route, or no fallback when the router is unsure.
rag-q56.spoken:
"The router's job is to send each question to the source that can answer it: computation over records goes to SQL, questions about our own documents go to the document index, and current or external facts go to web search. Some questions need two — 'which region had the most refunds, and what's our refund policy there?' — so the router can also decompose.

I'd use two tiers. A semantic router first: embed the query and compare it against labelled example utterances for each route, with a confidence threshold. It takes milliseconds and costs almost nothing, and it handles the confident majority. When the top score is low or two routes are close, escalate to an LLM router, which reads the query plus route descriptions and returns a structured decision — route, or routes plus sub-questions — validated against a schema.

Semantic routing wins on latency, cost and determinism, and it's easy to improve by adding examples. LLM routing wins on ambiguous, compositional or novel queries. Together: cheap for most traffic, smart where needed.

Guardrails: web search is untrusted input, with domain restrictions and injection handling; SQL runs read-only on curated views; and when confidence is low even after escalation, the system asks a clarifying question.

Every routing decision is logged, because a misroute poisons everything downstream — the best retriever can't answer from the wrong source."

stages.claim: the sources and their question types

Source Answers Example

document index policies, procedures, how-to "what's the refund policy in the EU?"
web search current external facts "what did the regulator announce this week?"

stages.claim: semantic in milliseconds, LLM in hundreds

LLM router: ~300–800 ms and tokens per call → reserve for the uncertain ~10–20% (illustrative)

followUps.html: Both: SQL for the top-5 by revenue, then the document index for each customer's contract renewal clause, merged. The router decomposes into two sub-questions.

followUps.html: It adds latency and cost on every query and is less predictable, while most queries are obvious. Use it as escalation.

followUps.question: How do you build the semantic router's examples?
followUps.html: From real queries labelled by route, plus synthetic variations; refreshed from logged misroutes.

rag-q57.testing: stable IDs, claim-level attribution, and verification of each citation.
rag-q57.trap: a list of "sources" appended at the end that nobody checked.
rag-q57.spoken:
"A decorative citation lists sources near the answer. A load-bearing citation ties each claim to the passage that supports it, and the system has checked that it does.

Three pieces make that work. Stable IDs: every chunk in the prompt carries an ID that maps back to a document, section and version — ideally a precise span or page — so a citation resolves to something a user can open.

Structured attribution: the model is asked to produce the answer as claims, each with the chunk IDs that support it — either inline markers or a structured output schema with a claims-and-sources list. Constrained output makes the format reliable.

Verification: after generation, each claim–citation pair is checked for entailment — does the cited passage actually support the claim? — with an NLI model or an LLM judge. Unsupported claims are removed, sent for revision once, or the answer abstains. A wrong citation is worse than none, because it lends false authority.

In the UI, citations open the exact passage highlighted, so users can verify in a click. And I measure citation precision — do cited passages support the claims — and citation recall — are all factual claims cited."

stages.claim: what must a citation let a user do?
stages.html: • Verify the claim in one click; know which version/date it came from.

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html: • Chunk IDs stable across re-indexing (document ID + section + version); page/offset metadata retained from parsing.

Deep-dive

💻 Prove it — the answer format that makes verification possible:

{
  "answer": "Pro includes 20 seats and costs $49/month.",
  "claims": [
    {"text": "Pro includes 20 seats.", "sources": ["pricing-2025#table-1"]},
    {"text": "Pro costs $49/month.",   "sources": ["pricing-2025#table-1"]}
  ]
}

Failure Cause

followUps.question: 🧪 The answer cites chunk 7 for "refunds within 30 days"; chunk 7 says "exchanges within 30 days". What should the verifier do?
followUps.html: Mark it unsupported (exchange ≠ refund) and either drop the claim, revise with the correct source, or abstain. That's exactly the error decorative citations hide.

followUps.question: "We list the retrieved documents under the answer."
followUps.html: That shows what was retrieved, not what supports which claim. Users can't verify, and unsupported claims look sourced.

followUps.question: Inline markers or structured claims?
followUps.html: Structured claims (JSON) are easiest to verify and render; inline markers read naturally. Many systems generate structured claims and render them as inline markers.

followUps.question: Is verification too slow?
followUps.html: A small NLI model checks pairs in tens of milliseconds; an LLM judge is slower. For streaming, verify after the stream completes and flag or edit, or verify only high-risk answers.

followUps.question: Where is this mandatory?
followUps.html: Legal, medical, finance, policy and compliance answers — anywhere a user acts on the answer. There, an answer without verified citations shouldn't be shown.

spine: How I use them by stage
rag-q58.testing: matching each metric to the question it answers and to the pipeline stage.
rag-q58.spoken:
"Each answers a different question.

Recall@k: of all the relevant chunks, what fraction made it into the top k? That's 'did the evidence make the pool?' — the key metric for the first-stage retriever that feeds a reranker.

Precision@k: of the top k, what fraction is relevant? That's 'how much junk comes with it?' — what matters for the chunks you actually send to the LLM.

Hit rate@k: did at least one relevant chunk appear in the top k? Useful when one chunk is enough to answer.

MRR, mean reciprocal rank: how high is the first relevant result, on average? One over its rank. It matters when the first result is what counts — search boxes, or systems that send very few chunks.

nDCG: grades the whole ordering, rewarding relevant items near the top and supporting graded relevance — 'highly relevant' vs 'somewhat'. Good for comparing rerankers.

So I pick by stage: recall@50 for the first-stage retriever, nDCG@10 or MRR for the reranker, precision@5 for what reaches the prompt, and end-to-end metrics after that. All of them need labelled relevant chunks per question — the golden set."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
Metric Question
recall@k did the evidence make the pool?
precision@k how much junk came with it?
hit rate@k was there at least one good chunk?
MRR how high was the first good chunk?
nDCG@k how good is the whole ordering (graded)?

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
💻 Prove it:

import math
rel = {"c3", "c7"}                              # relevant chunks for one query
ranked = ["c1", "c3", "c5", "c9", "c7"]         # retriever output
k = 5
hits = [c in rel for c in ranked[:k]]
recall = sum(hits) / len(rel); precision = sum(hits) / k
mrr = next((1 / (i + 1) for i, h in enumerate(hits) if h), 0)
dcg = sum(h / math.log2(i + 2) for i, h in enumerate(hits)); idcg = sum(1 / math.log2(i + 2) for i in range(len(rel)))
print(f"recall@5 {recall:.2f}  precision@5 {precision:.2f}  MRR {mrr:.2f}  nDCG@5 {dcg / idcg:.2f}  hit@5 {int(any(hits))}")
# → recall@5 1.00  precision@5 0.40  MRR 0.50  nDCG@5 0.62  hit@5 1

Perfect recall, but the first relevant chunk is 2nd (MRR 0.5) and the second is 5th — nDCG 0.62 says the ordering could be much better: a reranker's job.

stages.name: Where each misleads
stages.claim: each metric has a blind spot
stages.html:
• Recall@k with huge k looks great and says nothing about what reaches the prompt.
  • Precision@k is capped when few chunks are relevant (2 relevant → max precision@5 = 0.4).
  • MRR ignores everything after the first hit.
  • Hit rate hides multi-chunk questions that need several pieces.
  • All are only as good as the relevance labels.

stages.name: How I use them by stage
stages.claim: recall for retrieval, nDCG for ranking
stages.html:
Stage Metric
first-stage retrieval (dense/BM25/hybrid) recall@50/100
reranker nDCG@10, MRR
context sent to LLM precision@5, recall@5
end to end groundedness, answer correctness (Q59)

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Retrieval metrics need chunk labels; the triad evaluates generation with or without them (Q59).

followUps.question: 🧪 A query has exactly one relevant chunk. What's the maximum precision@10?
followUps.html: 0.1. Precision@k is bounded by (number relevant) / k, which is why it's misleading for single-answer questions; use MRR or hit rate there.

followUps.question: "Our recall@100 is 0.98, retrieval is great."
followUps.html: That says the evidence is somewhere in 100 candidates. What reaches the LLM depends on ranking; check recall@5 or nDCG@10 after reranking.

followUps.question: Why nDCG for rerankers?
followUps.html: It rewards putting the most relevant items first and supports graded relevance, matching what a reranker is supposed to improve.

followUps.question: How do you get relevance labels?
followUps.html: From the golden set: the chunk each synthetic question was generated from, plus human labels for real queries; LLM-judged relevance for scale, calibrated on a human sample (Q61).

followUps.question: Which single number would you put on a dashboard?
followUps.html: None alone: recall@50 for the retriever and nDCG@10 for the ranking stage, plus groundedness end to end — each owned by the team that can move it.

rag-q59.testing: the three edges of the question–context–answer triangle, and claim decomposition plus verification.
rag-q59.trap: treating a RAGAS score as ground truth.
rag-q59.spoken:
"The triad evaluates the three edges of the triangle between question, retrieved context and answer.

Context relevance, question to context: is what we retrieved relevant to the question? Low means a retrieval or ranking problem. Groundedness, or faithfulness, context to answer: is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? Low means the generator is adding things. Answer relevance, answer to question: does the answer actually address what was asked? Low means it's evasive, off-topic or answering a different question.

RAGAS computes faithfulness in two LLM steps. First, an LLM breaks the answer into atomic claims — short standalone statements. Second, for each claim, an LLM judges whether the retrieved context supports it. Faithfulness is the number of supported claims divided by the total. Answer relevancy works differently: an LLM generates questions the answer would answer, and their embedding similarity to the original question is measured. Context precision and recall compare retrieved chunks against reference answers or labels when you have them.

The caveats: every score is itself an LLM judgement, with its own errors and biases; it depends on the judge model and prompt version; and faithfulness says nothing about whether the context was correct. So I calibrate the judge against human labels on a sample and pin its version before trusting it for gates."

stages.name: The one-line claim
How it works
stages.html:
Metric Computation (typical)
faithfulness LLM splits answer into claims → LLM checks each against context → supported / total
answer relevancy LLM generates questions from the answer → mean embedding similarity to original question
context precision are relevant chunks ranked high (needs reference/labels or LLM relevance)
context recall can reference-answer statements be attributed to the context (needs reference)

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
claims = [("The Pro plan costs $49/month.", True), ("It includes 20 seats.", True), ("SSO is included on all plans.", False), ("Annual billing gives a 20% discount.", False)]
supported = sum(ok for _, ok in claims)
print(f"faithfulness = {supported}/{len(claims)} = {supported / len(claims):.2f}")
# → faithfulness = 2/4 = 0.50

The booleans stand in for the judge's verdicts; in RAGAS both the decomposition and the verdicts come from LLM calls.

stages.name: What it costs or misses
stages.html:
• Several LLM calls per evaluated answer (cost, latency, rate limits).
  • Judge errors and biases; sensitivity to judge model and prompt versions.
  • Faithful to a wrong context still scores high; correctness needs references.
  • Claim decomposition quality varies (too coarse or too fine).

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html: • Use the triad to localise failures (Q18); calibrate judges on human labels; pin versions; use reference-based correctness where labels exist.

followUps.question: 🧪 Faithfulness 0.95, answer relevance 0.40. What's wrong?
followUps.html: The answer is well supported by the context but doesn't address the question — often a query-understanding or retrieval-of-the-wrong-topic issue. Look at query rewriting and context relevance.

followUps.question: "RAGAS says 0.9 faithfulness, so the answers are correct."
followUps.html: It says claims are supported by the retrieved text, per an LLM judge. If the context is outdated or wrong, faithful answers are wrong. And the judge itself needs validation.

followUps.question: Why decompose into claims?
followUps.html: A long answer can be partly supported; atomic claims make the judgement per statement simpler and more reliable, and give a proportion instead of a yes/no.

followUps.question: Can you compute faithfulness without an LLM?
followUps.html: Partly, with NLI models checking entailment between sentences and context — cheaper and more consistent, less flexible with paraphrase and multi-sentence support.

followUps.question: How do you make these metrics trustworthy enough to gate releases?
followUps.html: Human-label a few hundred samples, measure judge–human agreement per metric, pin judge model/prompt versions, and gate on changes with confidence intervals rather than absolute scores (Q60).

rag-q60.testing: judge biases, calibration against humans, and using judges for regressions rather than absolute truth.
rag-q60.trap: great scores taken as great quality.
rag-q60.spoken:
"Because a judge score is a learned metric, and I haven't measured how well it agrees with the people whose judgement it's supposed to replace.

There are known biases. Verbosity: longer answers score higher. Position: in pairwise comparisons, the first or second answer is favoured. Self-preference: judges rate outputs from their own model family higher. Leniency: many judges give high scores to fluent answers regardless of subtle errors, especially in domains they don't know. And sensitivity: small changes to the rubric or judge model version move scores.

Great scores could also be a fake in the setup: the judge might not see the retrieved context, so it grades plausibility instead of faithfulness; the eval set might be too easy or leaked into prompts.

So before trusting it, I calibrate: a few hundred examples labelled by domain experts, the judge run on the same items, and agreement measured with kappa or correlation — compared with how much the experts agree with each other. Then I fix the design: specific rubrics per criterion, binary or three-point scales, pairwise comparisons in both orders, a judge from a different model family, reference answers where possible, and pinned judge versions.

Even then, I use the judge to detect regressions between versions, not to declare absolute quality, and I keep sampling human reviews."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "High judge scores mean the judge liked the answers; whether that tracks correctness is unmeasured."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Fake Check
judge doesn't see context inspect the judge prompt
easy or leaked eval set include hard, adversarial, unanswerable items
ceiling effect score distribution bunched at the top
same model as generator self-preference

stages.name: Confirm with calibration
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — the calibration table (cells to measure):

Criterion judge–human agreement (κ) human–human (κ) decision
faithfulness measure measure gate if close to human–human
answer relevance measure measure
tone measure measure monitor only if low
  • Also: length–score correlation (verbosity), order-swap consistency (position).

stages.name: Fix by design
stages.html:
• Per-criterion rubrics with anchored examples; binary/3-point scales; reasoning before score.
  • Order-swapped pairwise comparisons; different-family judge; reference-guided grading.
  • Pin judge model and prompt versions; re-calibrate on changes.

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: gate only where it agrees with humans
stages.html: • Gate on judge metrics only where agreement is close to human–human; weekly human sample; compare judge trends with user feedback.

followUps.question: 🧪 Judge scores rose 8 points after a prompt change that made answers 35% longer. Suspicion?
followUps.html: Verbosity bias. Check length-controlled comparisons and a human sample before believing the gain.

followUps.question: "92% average score — quality is great."
followUps.html: Absolute judge scores aren't calibrated to quality; many judges are lenient. Use them for relative comparisons after calibration.

followUps.question: Why kappa rather than percent agreement?
followUps.html: It corrects for agreement by chance; with skewed labels (most answers good), percent agreement is high even for a useless judge.

followUps.question: Why a different model family as judge?
followUps.html: To reduce self-preference bias, where a judge favours outputs similar to its own style.

followUps.question: What does the judge gate, and what doesn't it?
followUps.html: It gates regressions on criteria where it's calibrated (e.g. faithfulness); it doesn't decide absolute launch readiness, new domains or safety-critical outputs — those need human review.
